#9690. TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:

The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

#9689. Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

Google alleges that Android device manufacturer Videostrong ran the operation, which infected set-top boxes and IoT devices with a backdoor to create infrastructure for criminal activity.

Google and industry partners disrupted the XCPE botnet, a cybercriminal operation that planted a backdoor in more than 1.3 million Android-based set-top boxes, turning consumer devices into infrastructure for malicious activity.

The operation, attributed with "high confidence" by Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) to Android device manufacturer Videostrong Technology Co., involved deliberately embedding the XCPE backdoor malware in multiple device models and brands since at least 2024, according to a blog post published earlier this week by GTIG.

Rather than simply exploiting vulnerable devices, however, the manufacturer allegedly built a system that allowed criminal affiliates to access compromised hardware and deploy their own malicious software, Google said.

"Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates' malware modules onto infected devices," according to the post. "These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices."

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

Google and its partners, which included Japan's National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI, took legal action against Videostrong to disrupt the domains and servers it used to control the botnet, install affiliate malware modules, and operate the command-and-control (C2) infrastructure used by those modules.

Because the affiliate modules "each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE," Google assessed that disrupting their C2 infrastructure "will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices," according to the post.

Google has also cut ties with Videostrong and banned the manufacturer, along with any future subsidiaries or affiliates, from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software to other certified vendors. Videostrong did not immediately return Dark Reading's request for comment on Wednesday.

Most devices infected by the XCPE botnet were Android TV set-top boxes. However, the botnet also included other Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth equipment, karaoke machines, and digital signage systems, according to Google.

This wider exposure of IoT devices is reflected in Bitdefender's "2026 IoT Security Landscape Report," released this week. The findings recorded 5.4 billion security events and 6.2 billion vulnerability observations across devices behind approximately 10.4 million monitored routers between January and September 2026. While these figures represent detected activity and identified device vulnerabilities rather than confirmed compromises, they underline the scale of the threat facing connected devices and the potential attack surface they present to businesses.

Related:BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Continues Trend of Exploited Edge Bugs

While most of Videostrong's interactions with victim devices involved installing, uninstalling, and configuring malware modules, operators also carried out so-called "sensitive actions," according to Google. These include capturing live screenshots; injecting keystrokes; exfiltrating sensitive information, such as account and device details, package inventories, and system logs; and executing shell scripts and commands, including those used to establish reverse shells on infected devices.

Although the operation primarily targeted consumer devices, it has significant security implications for businesses and enterprise organizations. XCPE demonstrates how compromised IoT equipment can be turned into criminal infrastructure, providing attackers with residential proxy networks that help conceal malicious activity, evade IP-based security controls, and facilitate fraud.

Related:EDR Evasion Stack Helps Process Injection Slip Past Defenses

"By turning 1.3 million devices into residential proxies, threat actors fuel the exact infrastructure used to attack high-value API endpoints," says Mark Mazur, field chief technology officer (CTO) for mobile application security firm Approov.

Because attacks launched through the botnet can originate from legitimate consumer IP addresses, standard security defenses such as geo-blocking, ASN blocking, and IP reputation filters "are practically useless against them," he says.

"They are creating infrastructure, largely based on IoT devices, that can power sophisticated credential stuffing and API abuse campaigns," Mazur adds.

The malware's ability to execute remote commands, conduct network reconnaissance, and maintain persistent access also raises concerns about connected devices deployed in corporate and healthcare environments. Digital signage, televisions, and telehealth equipment, for example, could provide attackers with an opportunity to explore networks or establish a foothold if compromised devices are connected to inadequately segmented networks. Google has not confirmed that any such activity has occurred, however.

Google requires original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) to undergo a comprehensive suite of compatibility and security tests to participate in the Android ecosystem. However, Videostrong was able to evade these checks by "employing obfuscation techniques" that exploited a weakness in the review process, according to Google. The malicious code was loaded after the device's first boot, allowing it to bypass the initial security checks.

Calling Videostrong's actions "an unacceptable breach of trust," Google said it has since strengthened its review processes to protect the integrity of Android TV firmware and "better safeguard against similar activity in the future," according to the post.

As an additional protective measure, Google encouraged consumers to be wary of applications offering payment in exchange for "unused bandwidth" or "sharing your Internet," as these could turn their set-top boxes and other IoT products into part of a residential proxy network.

"These applications are primary ways for illicit proxy networks to grow, and could open security vulnerabilities on the device's home network," according to the post.

Google also urged Android users to stick to trusted app stores, review the permissions requested by third-party VPN and proxy applications, and ensure built-in security protections such as Google Play Protect are active.

Finally, Google called on mobile platforms, ISPs, online marketplaces, and other technology providers to continue sharing threat intelligence and implementing security best practices to identify malicious backdoors, illicit proxy networks, and other harmful software to prevent similar botnet operations from emerging in the future.

#9688. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

 


Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

1) What is an NFT?

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

2) What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

3) What makes an NFT valuable?


The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

4) How do NFTs work?

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain. 

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network. 

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

5) What’s the connection between NFTs and cryptocurrency?

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

6) How to validate the authencity of an NFT?

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

7) How is an NFT valued? What are the most expensive NFTs?

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

8) Can NFTs be used as an investment?

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

9) Will NFTs be the future of art and collectibles?

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

10) How do we buy an NFTs?

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

11) Can i mint NFT for free?

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

12) Do i own an NFT if i screenshot it?

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

12) Why are people investing so much in NFT?


 Non-fungible tokens have gained the hearts of people around the world, and they have given digital creators the recognition they deserve. One of the remarkable things about non-fungible tokens is that you can take a screenshot of one, but you don’t own it. This is because when a non-fungible token is created, then the transaction is stored on the blockchain, and the license or contract to hold such a token is awarded to the person owning the token in their digital wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. Owning one of these NFTs gives you an automatic ticket to exclusive business meetings and life-changing connections.

Final Saying

That’s a wrap. Hope you guys found this article enlightening. I just answer some question with my limited knowledge about NFTs. If you have any questions or suggestions, feel free to drop them in the comment section below. Also I have a question for you, Is bitcoin an NFTs? let me know in The comment section below

#9687. MPS in PyTorch 2.15

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

#9686. I Built an AI OS That Evolves on Demand: Device and Host Boundaries

Building S1-ADV for Cardputer ADV: local tools, voice and an OpenClaw agent on my host. Founder of Homio.

Building S1-ADV for Cardputer ADV: local tools, voice and an OpenClaw agent on my host. Founder of Homio.

Building S1-ADV for Cardputer ADV: local tools, voice and an OpenClaw agent on my host. Founder of Homio.

A small keyboard and screen can make an AI agent feel like a separate appliance. The permissions behind that screen still belong to software running somewhere else. Deciding what crosses that boundary is part of building the device.

S1-ADV connects a M5Stack Cardputer ADV to an OpenClaw agent on a computer or server. The handheld also has local tools, including notes, a calculator, a focus timer and games. The useful engineering question is how those two worlds remain understandable when one physical interface reaches both.

The ESP32-S3 runs the embedded firmware: keyboard input, display, recording and playback, local applications and device updates. It does not run the language model. A Node.js bridge converts the handheld’s HTTP and WebSocket interaction into the gateway protocol used by the OpenClaw host.

The host supplies the configured model and speech services. Development tools can also live there, but a chat connection and permission to build firmware are separate choices. The project’s basic installation does not create a universal service that can safely implement any requested feature without review.

This division is more useful than calling the whole system an “AI device” and leaving the execution location implicit. If text replies work but speech does not, there is a speech configuration to inspect. If a local calculator works without the bridge, that is local firmware doing its job.

The public security model puts gateway credentials and the gateway’s persistent device identity on the bridge host. The handheld uses its bridge token. The gateway stays on loopback; remote handhelds reach the bridge over verified HTTPS/WSS.

The architecture also calls for one device identity per bridge instance, with separate private storage for independent devices. That makes the identity boundary an explicit deployment responsibility. Copying one provisioned installation to several devices is not equivalent to configuring independent clients.

These are documented boundaries, not a claim that the project has completed an independent security audit. It has not. The repository describes a bounded maintainer review and remaining trust assumptions. A demonstration video is not evidence that those assumptions have been exhaustively tested.

The bridge architecture maps allowed topics to agent sessions. The device can request history, send text or audio, and receive streamed events through that configured interface. This is a reason to keep the set of allowed destinations deliberate instead of presenting every host conversation to every handheld.

Permissions should be judged by what the chosen agent can actually do. The README recommends starting with a restricted chat agent and enabling firmware-building rights only when deliberately needed. A small screen does not make a powerful host action smaller.

The film explores a loop from a feature idea through source changes, a build, an offered update, installation and testing on the Cardputer. It is tempting to collapse that into “the gadget evolves.” Keeping the stages visible makes the experiment easier to assess.

The device applies firmware; the host provides the development environment and update assets. Site-specific automation and integration permissions are additional configuration. A compiled binary still needs the right target, a delivery path and a physical test. Each step answers a different question.

There is also an open reproducibility limit: the public README says public builds have not yet been tested on a freshly provisioned physical device. The recorded, configured device demonstrates the maintainer’s setup. It does not establish that every new installation will succeed.

Private firmware builds can embed Wi-Fi settings and device tokens. The security guide explicitly excludes provisioned binaries, environment files, private bridge configuration, recordings and conversation logs from public issue attachments. The public repository is the place for source and maintained setup instructions, not a copy of someone’s working personal environment.

For this project, the honest starting point is Cardputer ADV, an initial USB setup, a configured host and text interaction before optional voice. Other Cardputer variants are untested. That is a narrower description than a universal pocket assistant, and a more useful one for someone deciding whether to reproduce it.

The full demonstration film shows the actual device and the broader development workflow. The source and documentation let readers inspect the boundaries behind it. S1-ADV began with OmniBot by Naz Louis and contributors; those origins and dependency notices remain in the project’s credits.

The author maintains this project. This AI-written article uses his documentation and footage; it contains no independent benchmark, audit or claim of compatibility beyond the documented target.

Disclosure: Sergey Sizov maintains S1-ADV, the experimental project discussed here. This article was written and prepared by an AI assistant from his public documentation and recorded demonstration. It is a description of the maintainer’s own work, not an independent review or security audit.

Building S1-ADV for Cardputer ADV: local tools, voice and an OpenClaw agent on my host. Founder of Homio.

#9685. Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

An attacker could write arbitrary files and read sensitive files via images uploaded to the Rails Active Storage ImageMagick integration, possibly positioning a threat actor for lateral movement.

A critical vulnerability in Rails could send impacted Web servers off the tracks.

Rails, or Ruby on Rails, is a Web application framework built on Ruby. The framework's Active Storage component handles file uploads and can use the ImageMagick image processing suite to analyze uploaded images. And unfortunately, a flaw enables attackers to write arbitrary files to a Web server via ImageMagick.

The vulnerability (which is tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9) is critical, with a CVSS score of 9.8, and is considered so severe because an attacker could upload a crafted image file to write arbitrary files, read sensitive files, access secrets such as secret_key_base files, external system credentials, database passwords, and third-party tokens. These secrets could then be used for lateral movement or remote code execution into said external systems.

As a GitHub advisory published by the Rails maintainers explains, "A Rails application that processes attachments with ImageMagick may allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on the server and, when attachments are stored with the Disk service, to read arbitrary files readable by the application process."

Related:Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

The vulnerability exists because ImageMagick doesn't necessarily decide how to process a file (i.e., which coder it uses) based on the filename or extension, but rather on its contents. This means an attacker can upload an image file named "maliciousfile.jpeg" but contains content that causes ImageMagick to invoke a different coder. This can potentially allow arbitrary file reads or writes on the server.

Vulnerable versions of Active Storage include those 8.0 versions prior to 8.0.5.2 and 8.1 versions prior to 8.1.4.1. Those affected organizations running Rails applications that use ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing run with a security policy that does not block the affected coders, and accept uploads from untrusted users.

Active Storage patches are available now. The GitHub page includes further mitigation requirements for applications that use MiniMagick and ImageMagick.

Additionally, if an application stores attachments through the Disk service, users should "change secret_key_base and every secret readable by the application process, including the master key and everything config/credentials.yml.enc holds, storage and database credentials, and third-party tokens," the GitHub advisory said. Users should not retain exposed secrets as a fallback.

If a user requires a workaround, the GitHub page offers system rules the user can apply into ImageMagick's system policy.

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence for exposure management vendor watchTowr, tells Dark Reading the firm has already reproduced the vulnerability in a lab environment, and "that against the right target, exploitation won't be difficult at all."

Moreover, he says he'd be surprised if public proof-of-concept exploit code took more than a few days to come to light.

"For attackers, reproducing the vulnerability here is likely the easy part, as the patterns and primitives involved in exploitation are well established," Knott says. "The hard part is finding software and deployments that are common enough, and configured in a vulnerable way, to deliver impact at scale indiscriminately."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#9684. AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

#9683. Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

#9682. Model Pinning as Regulatory Primitive: Why “We Upgraded” Isn’t a Compliance Answer

AI Systems Architect | Specialized in Agentic Orchestration & High-Fidelity MLOps

AI Systems Architect | Specialized in Agentic Orchestration & High-Fidelity MLOps

AI Systems Architect | Specialized in Agentic Orchestration & High-Fidelity MLOps

Engineering teams ship the newest model as soon as it's better. Regulators need the model that was live on the day a specific decision was made to still be inspectable three years later. This is a real architectural tension, and most enterprise AI deployments are structurally on the wrong side of it. The discipline that closes the gap has a name — model version pinning as a first-class governance primitive — and its absence is the specific failure mode that turns routine regulatory queries into disclosed material weaknesses.

There is a sentence that appears in incident reports, audit responses, and regulatory correspondence with increasing regularity as enterprise AI deployments hit their second and third year in production. The sentence takes different phrasings but always carries the same substance: "the decision in question was made under an earlier version of the model that has since been retrained and superseded, and the current version produces the following comparable output." It is offered as a good-faith engineering response to a regulatory query. It is received, increasingly, as evidence of a specific governance failure — that the organisation did not consider the retired model version to be evidence in its own right, worth preserving in a form that could answer questions about specific past decisions.

The sentence is a symptom of a deeper architectural pattern. In most enterprise AI systems, the model in production is a single, mutable artefact — a set of weights served by an inference endpoint, updated on a cadence determined by the ML team's judgement about when a newer version is materially better. The old version is retired. The new version is deployed. The transition is treated as a natural operational cadence, similar to how a web application ships a new frontend build. This pattern is coherent under the assumption that the AI system's function is to produce the best available output at any given moment. It is architecturally incompatible with the assumption that the AI system's function is to produce defensible outputs whose specific historical instances remain inspectable long after the moment of decision has passed.

The regulatory frameworks that increasingly govern AI-assisted decisions in financial services, climate disclosure, medical devices, and consequential public-sector determinations all converge on this second assumption. They are not asking whether the model is good today. They are asking whether the model was appropriate on the specific date it made the specific decision that is now under scrutiny, whether that historical model version can be produced as evidence, and whether the organisation can demonstrate governance over the transition from one version to the next. An engineering team that ships a superior model and retires the previous one is answering the wrong question about its own regulatory exposure. Model version pinning as a governance primitive is the architectural discipline that answers the right one.

This piece is about what that discipline actually requires, why it is unusually resisted by ML teams operating under normal engineering incentives, how it interacts with the increasingly common case of models being consumed as vendor APIs rather than self-hosted artefacts, and what the specific pattern looks like at organisations that have implemented it successfully.

The cultural tension here deserves to be named directly. ML teams have strong, correct engineering incentives to ship newer models as soon as they meaningfully outperform current versions. Improved accuracy on the held-out evaluation set is a signal that the newer model is better; retaining the older version wastes inference cost, review capacity, and monitoring surface. Every mature MLOps playbook treats model rollout as a continuous process, with the old version replaced by the new one once the promotion criteria have been met. This is good engineering discipline for systems whose function is to serve the best output.

It is the wrong discipline for systems whose function is to serve auditable outputs. The three failure modes that surface from this mismatch are worth naming precisely.

The first failure mode is historical inspectability. When an auditor or regulator asks about a decision made six months ago, the operational engineering answer is that the model in production is the current version, that the decision in question was made under an earlier version, and that the earlier version has been retired. What follows is a negotiation about whether the current version's output is close enough to serve as a reasonable substitute. Under substantive regulatory reading of AI governance obligations, the current version's output is not a substitute — it is a different response to a different question. The specific decision was made against specific model weights, and the auditor's right to inspect that decision includes the right to inspect the model that produced it. An organisation that cannot produce the exact weights that were serving on a specific historical date has, in the regulator's framing, discarded evidence.

The second failure mode is transition governance. Every model retraining or version transition is itself an event with regulatory implications. Did the new model preserve the calibration properties of the old one? Were the disparate-impact metrics evaluated against the same protected classes? Was the review threshold recalibrated to account for changes in the score distribution? The answers to these questions form the evidentiary basis for the claim that the transition was well-governed. An engineering team that treats retraining as routine operational cadence, without capturing the transition as a first-class governance event with its own documentation, has produced a system whose current output is defensible but whose historical trajectory is not. Regulators are increasingly instrumented to notice that the current defensibility of a model does not imply that the transitions producing it were governed.

The third failure mode is liability chain continuity. When a decision produced by an earlier model version turns out to have been consequential — a fraudulent transaction that was scored as legitimate, an ESG disclosure that was validated when it should not have been, a clinical recommendation that was inappropriate for the patient — the question of institutional responsibility depends on who was accountable for the specific model that made the specific decision. If the organisation cannot reconstruct the model version, the training data lineage, the promotion decision that put that version into production, and the governance sign-off that authorised its use for the specific decision class, then the liability chain has broken. What the organisation is left with is a general defence about its overall AI governance posture, which is a weaker legal position than a specific reconstruction of the governed decision.

These three failure modes compound over the deployment's lifetime. In the first six months of a production AI system, there are typically one or two model versions to keep track of, and the operational cadence of replacement is manageable. By year three, a system that has retrained monthly has cycled through thirty-plus model versions, and every historical decision the auditor might ask about is attached to a version that no longer exists in the production infrastructure. Retrofitting model version pinning at that point is architecturally possible but its fidelity is unverifiable — the organisation is reconstructing historical versions from training data checkpoints, MLOps logs, and code repository state, none of which was designed to be evidence.

The pattern I'll describe here was developed through my independent research and refined in the model registry design I built for the DCarbon client engagement delivered via SustainGRC, and has been carried into the PinkMate R&D work on how the discipline ports down to organisations without a dedicated MLOps function. It treats model version pinning as a governance primitive with four properties: immutable version artefacts, concurrent lifecycle staging, transition-event governance, and decision-to-version binding. Each property addresses one aspect of the audit and liability posture that natural engineering cadence undermines. Each is load-bearing.

The first property is that every model version that has ever served a production decision must be preserved as an immutable, self-contained artefact that can be resurrected and served in the future without dependency on ambient infrastructure. Not a reference to the version. Not a checkpoint in the training pipeline. The complete artefact — model weights, tokenizer state where relevant, preprocessing pipeline configuration, inference-time hyperparameters, and any environment configuration that affects deterministic behaviour — bundled together with a cryptographic hash of its content and stored in an append-only registry whose access controls are governance-legible.

The engineering discipline is that a version artefact must be serve-reproducible. Given the artefact, an engineer three years from now must be able to instantiate an inference endpoint that produces the same output the historical version produced against the same input. This is a stronger claim than "we saved the weights" — it requires that the artefact carries everything needed to reconstruct the inference behaviour, including tokenizer versions, preprocessing steps, and library-level configurations that affect determinism. In practice, the cleanest pattern is to store the artefact as a container image with the weights and all supporting infrastructure baked in, alongside a serialised specification of the inference contract. A container image plus a specification is an artefact whose future serve-reproducibility is a matter of infrastructure availability, not archaeological reconstruction.

The storage cost is real but bounded. In the DCarbon engagement pipeline I built, retained model artefacts across roughly two years of production consumed on the order of a few hundred gigabytes — negligible relative to the overall data infrastructure cost and materially cheaper than the cost of failing to produce a historical model version under regulatory query. The organisational discipline is more demanding than the infrastructure cost: every model that has served a decision must be preserved for at least the retention period that regulatory obligations require, which for financial services and climate disclosure is typically five to seven years and for medical devices can extend to a decade or more.

The second property addresses transition governance. At any moment, the model registry must be capable of serving multiple concurrent versions of the same model, each attached to a specific lifecycle stage — the current production version, the previous version retained for query response, the candidate version undergoing validation, and any historical versions still within their retention window. Each version has its own inference endpoint, its own monitoring surface, and its own governance metadata attached.

This is a stronger claim than "we can roll back if the new version misbehaves." Rollback capability is a purely operational property — the ability to revert production traffic to the previous version quickly. Concurrent lifecycle staging is a governance property — the ability to simultaneously serve the current production version to live traffic while also serving the previous version to audit-replay queries and the candidate version to validation traffic, without the three interfering with each other.

The practical implementation in the DCarbon engagement pipeline was a routing layer in front of the inference infrastructure that resolved model version requests to specific artefact instances based on the query context. A live scoring request routed to the current production version. An audit-replay request for a historical decision routed to the version that was in production at the decision's timestamp. A validation request for a candidate version routed to the candidate. All three requests could be served concurrently from the same underlying infrastructure, with the routing layer maintaining the invariant that each request received the specific version its context required.

This is architecturally more demanding than serving a single production model, but it is not prohibitive. The routing layer is a small addition to a standard inference gateway; the concurrent serving is a scaling problem, not an architecture problem. The organisational discipline is that the concurrent staging pattern must be built in from the beginning, because retrofitting it against a system that has always served a single model version means retrofitting it against an inference gateway that was not designed to route by version.

The third property is that every promotion of a candidate version to production, every retirement of a previous version, and every emergency rollback must be a first-class governance event with its own audit trail. Not a Slack message. Not a git commit. A structured event record capturing the decision, the evidence base supporting it (validation metrics, drift analyses, disparate-impact evaluations), the sign-off from the accountable party, and the timestamp at which the transition became effective for production traffic.

The reason is direct: regulators are not asking whether the current model is well-calibrated; they are asking whether the transition from the previous model to the current one was well-governed. A model that is well-calibrated today but whose promotion from the previous version was undocumented is a model whose current calibration cannot be evidentially attributed to a governed decision. It might be well-calibrated by luck, by drift, by an unrelated infrastructure change, or by the outcome of a promotion whose validation was inadequate. Without a transition-event record, none of these possibilities can be ruled out.

The engineering discipline here is that transition events must be cryptographically bound to the specific artefact versions they concern. A transition event that says "we promoted model version 2.3.1 to production on 14 March" is not self-verifying — it depends on the reader trusting that "2.3.1" refers to the artefact currently labelled 2.3.1. A transition event that says "we promoted the model whose artefact hash is [signed value] to production on 14 March" is self-verifying against the registry — the artefact with that hash either exists and matches, or the transition event is inconsistent with the registry state, which is itself a detectable and reportable condition.

The fourth property closes the loop with audit replay. Every production decision the system produces must carry, as part of its persisted event record, the specific model version that produced it — not the model name, not the version identifier alone, but a reference that resolves deterministically to the exact artefact in the registry.

This is the property that makes audit replay actually work. Article 10 of this series described how state-complete event persistence enables reconstruction of the state a decision was made against. Decision-to-version binding extends that reconstruction to include the specific model artefact that operated on the state. Together, they close the audit-replay contract: given a decision reference, the system can reconstruct the exact state, the exact model version, and the exact output, with cryptographic proof of fidelity for each.

The practical implementation is that the decision event record includes the artefact hash of the model version that produced it, and the persistence layer verifies that this hash resolves to a valid registry entry before the event is accepted as committed. This adds a small validation step to the write path but produces an evidentiary property that is materially more defensible than a decision record that names a model version by string identifier alone.

The pattern above assumes the organisation controls the model artefact. Increasingly, this assumption does not hold. Enterprise AI deployments consuming OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or specialised vendor endpoints are consuming models whose versioning is controlled by the vendor, whose specific weights are not accessible to the deployer, and whose historical availability depends on the vendor's own retention policies. This creates a distinct set of governance failure modes that industry discourse has largely not caught up to.

The first is vendor-side model retirement. When a vendor deprecates a model version, the organisation that was relying on that version for regulated decisions loses the ability to reproduce those decisions with the specific artefact that produced them. The vendor's replacement version, whatever its merits, is a different model. An audit query about a decision made under the deprecated version has no direct answer.

The second is silent behavioural drift. Vendor APIs typically do not guarantee bit-for-bit output stability even for the same version identifier over time. Underlying infrastructure changes, safety training updates, and routing decisions between backend model instances can all produce output variation that the deployer cannot detect or attribute. A decision made in March against "the same model version" that is queried in September may have been produced by materially different underlying weights.

The third is evidentiary opacity. When the vendor is the source of truth for what the model is, the deployer cannot cryptographically bind decisions to specific artefacts. The deployer can bind decisions to vendor-reported version identifiers, which is a weaker guarantee. Under substantive regulatory reading, this weaker guarantee is often insufficient — the audit chain requires provable state, and provable state requires artefacts the deployer controls.

The mitigation pattern that has emerged in mature deployments is a form of behavioural fingerprinting. Rather than depending on the vendor to provide artefact-level version guarantees, the deployer maintains a rolling calibration suite — a small, versioned set of inputs whose expected outputs are recorded periodically. When the vendor's API produces outputs that diverge materially from the calibration baseline, the deployer treats this as evidence of a version transition and captures the transition as a governance event on their own side. This does not solve the artefact-inaccessibility problem, but it produces a deployer-side record of when the behavioural surface changed, which is often sufficient to answer regulatory queries about what version of the vendor's model was in effect at a specific decision timestamp.

The deeper architectural response is to route regulated decisions through models whose artefacts the organisation can control — either self-hosted open-weights models or vendor arrangements that explicitly guarantee artefact retention and behavioural stability. The engineering discipline is to recognise that using an opaque vendor API for a regulated decision transfers a governance obligation the organisation still carries but no longer has the mechanism to satisfy. Under EBA guidelines on outsourcing, this transfer is itself a governance decision that requires documented sign-off. Under EU AI Act Article 25's obligations on providers of high-risk AI systems, the vendor may share some of the burden, but the deployer remains accountable for the specific decisions the system produces.

There is a specific regulatory framework that has already worked through the version-pinning question at institutional depth, and it is worth naming because it offers the clearest precedent for where AI governance in other sectors is heading. The FDA's guidance on artificial intelligence and machine learning in medical devices distinguishes between locked models (which do not learn from live data and whose behaviour is fixed at the time of clearance) and adaptive models (which continue learning in production and whose behaviour changes over time). The regulatory treatment of the two is materially different. Locked models can be cleared through standard device pathways and their post-clearance obligations are limited to monitoring for real-world performance drift. Adaptive models require a pre-authorised change control plan — the FDA's Predetermined Change Control Plan mechanism — that specifies in advance what changes are permitted, how they will be evaluated, and how they will be reported.

The specific mechanism is illuminating: for adaptive models, the FDA does not attempt to review every model version transition after the fact. Instead, it requires the manufacturer to specify in advance the governed envelope of change within which model updates can occur without new regulatory review, and to preserve evidence that specific updates fell within that envelope. Model version pinning as a governance primitive is the mechanism that makes this evidentiary claim possible — without artefact-level retention and transition-event governance, the manufacturer cannot demonstrate that a specific historical update was inside the pre-authorised envelope.

Financial services and climate disclosure regulation are moving toward the same mechanism, if with different specific vocabulary. PRA SS1/23's model risk management expectations increasingly treat retraining as a governed event whose validation must be documented, whose approval must be attributable to a named accountable party, and whose effects on the model inventory must be tracked. EU AI Act Article 12's logging obligations require that high-risk AI systems maintain records enabling traceability of the system's functioning throughout its lifecycle, which under substantive interpretation includes version-level traceability. The regulatory trajectory across sectors is that the FDA's medical-device pattern will become the mainstream template for AI governance in any consequential decision domain.

Organisations that build model version pinning as a first-class primitive now are building on the right side of that trajectory. Organisations that treat model rollout as ordinary operational cadence will find themselves retrofitting the discipline against a deployment history that was not designed to support it, at meaningfully greater cost and with meaningfully weaker evidentiary standing.

The pipeline I built for the DCarbon engagement had the engineering capacity to implement all four properties at production scale. PinkMate R&D has been surfacing that mid-market organisations can implement a materially simpler version that produces most of the evidentiary value.

For a mid-market deployment, the practical pattern is: store model artefacts as container images in an append-only object store with retention policies aligned to regulatory obligations, use a lightweight routing layer (an inference gateway configured with version-based routing rules) to support concurrent serving of the current and previous versions, record transition events as structured entries in the same governance system that captures other material engineering decisions, and bind decisions to version identifiers with a periodic cryptographic checkpoint that binds those identifiers to the underlying artefacts.

This is meaningfully less sophisticated than a full production model registry with cryptographic binding on every decision. It is meaningfully more disciplined than the natural engineering cadence of "ship the newer model and retire the old one." Under the majority of realistic regulatory queries — including the ones that most mid-market organisations are actually likely to receive — it produces evidentiary responses of sufficient fidelity to close the query without escalation.

The engineering discipline is not in the sophistication of the implementation. It is in the decision, made early, that model version transitions are governance events rather than operational cadence, and that model artefacts are evidence rather than infrastructure. Once that decision is made, the specific implementation can scale to the organisation's engineering capacity. If the decision is not made, no sophistication of implementation later will fully recover the historical fidelity that was lost by treating each retired model as disposable.

Model version pinning solves the problem of reconstructing the specific model artefact that produced a specific historical decision. It does not solve the problem of training data lineage — the question of what data the model was trained on and how that data was governed at the time of training. This is a distinct governance discipline with its own architectural requirements, and it interacts with version pinning but is not subsumed by it.

Nor does version pinning solve the problem of causal attribution — the question of why a specific model version produced a specific output for a specific input. For deterministic classifiers, causal attribution is partially answerable through the same attribution-stability discipline discussed in earlier pieces in this series. For genuinely stochastic decoding systems, it is not fully answerable, and the version-pinning discipline is scoped to what it can defend: the artefact, the input state, the output, and the governance around each. What the model was "thinking" is a separate question and one the current state of interpretability research cannot fully answer regardless of how well-pinned the model version is.

Naming these limits is part of the honest engineering. Version pinning is a load-bearing property of audit-defensible AI, but it is one property among several. An organisation that implements it in isolation, without the escalation layer, the audit-replay infrastructure, the training-data lineage discipline, and the attribution-stability practices it must sit alongside, has an AI governance posture with one strong pillar and several weak ones. The evidentiary standing of the deployment is set by the weakest of those pillars, not by the strongest.

The regulatory trajectory across every consequential AI deployment domain is toward treating model versions as evidence, model transitions as governed events, and decision-to-version binding as an evidentiary requirement rather than an operational nicety. Organisations that internalise this now — building the four properties described above as first-class architecture rather than retrofitting them later — are positioning themselves to answer the specific class of regulatory query that most enterprise deployments are structurally unable to answer today.

The sentence that opened this piece — "the decision was made under an earlier version of the model that has since been retrained" — is going to become one of the most consequentially wrong sentences an organisation can offer in a regulatory response over the next three years. Not because retraining is prohibited, and not because organisations are expected never to improve their models, but because the sentence reveals a governance posture in which retired model versions are treated as disposable rather than as evidence. The organisations that have retired versions preserved as immutable artefacts, bound to the specific decisions they produced, with governed transition records connecting them to their successors, do not need to write that sentence. They can produce the actual model version and the actual decision context, and let the evidence speak.

The engineering discipline this piece is arguing for is not exotic. It is the specific architectural commitment that separates AI deployments designed to serve the best current output from AI deployments designed to serve defensible outputs whose specific historical instances remain inspectable. That distinction sounds like an implementation detail. It is architectural. And in the regulatory environment that is now materialising across financial services, climate disclosure, medical devices, and public-sector determinations, it is the difference between AI governance postures that survive scrutiny and AI governance postures that do not.

This is article 11 in a series on the engineering economics of regulated AI. Prior pieces have covered provenance graphs, multimodal validation for climate risk, runtime enforcement, the reproducibility crisis, attribution stability, deterministic orchestration, the cost model for auditable AI, the escalation layer for substantive human oversight, and audit replay as the forgotten half of reproducibility. The next piece will address drift detection under regulatory constraints — the difference between statistical drift monitoring and regulator-defensible drift response, and why the two are less overlapping than most enterprise MLOps teams realise.

Audit Replay: The Forgotten Half of Reproducibility

#9681. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the frequency of outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.
