#9651. nemotron-halloween

TL;DR: MonsterHouse is an interactive projection I created for Halloween. He listens to trick-or-treaters, answers in the voice of a grumpy old pirate ship and softens when visitors remember their manners. He is built on the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent with NVIDIA Nemotron ASR, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, Magpie TTS Zeroshot and Audio2Face-3D, and he runs on a single workstation.

I wanted the kids visiting my house at Halloween to interact in a fun and unique way. The house was going to be in charge and giving out the treats, but more grumpy than scary. Somehow, my solution was to give the garage door a mouth and teach him to complain.

That became MonsterHouse: a grumpy old building with pirate stories, a fiery grin and a suspicious weakness for “please.” NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent supplies the conversation foundation. Nemotron Speech does the listening, Bolt E4B is the brain, NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot is the live voice, and NVIDIA Audio2Face-3D makes the wooden mouth talk.

The mouth came first. I imagined the wooden garage door boards splitting into jagged lips, with the burning flames of hell illuminating the driveway from beyond whenever he opened his cursed mouth. He needed to look ancient, expressive and mildly offended by the existence of visitors.

A few expressions from a house with plenty to say.

Creating a custom animation rig was one of the more labor intensive parts of the build. After bashing it into submission, I could export the facial expression shapes that Audio2Face-3D could later animate. The character SkelMesh was built in Autodesk Maya then exported into Unreal Engine where virtual fire and effects were added behind the door. With no eyes, no eyebrows and no blinking, he’s a surprisingly economical monster.

While all the nonsense of building the character was going on, NVIDIA built the Nemotron Voice Agent. What was supposed to be the hard part of the build now became rather fun, iterative and easy. I had a foundation for listening, conversation and speech right out of the box. The house already had a mouth. Now he could finally find something to complain about.

The house needed a past as cantankerous as its personality so I devised a backstory that the house had been built from the timbers of a sunken pirate ship, haunted by its stormy past. The nautical complaints now had a reason. This was the ship, reincarnated as real estate and not entirely pleased about it.

The performance needed a guide, a path to follow from greeting to goodbye while providing treats along the way. First, the house would brush visitors off with remarks like “I’m busy grumbling, go bother the neighbors!” But persistence would wear him down. A “Please” could break through immediately, and “thank you” earned a warm farewell. Once a visitor won him over, I wanted him to stay won over. Nobody wants to negotiate with the same garage door twice.

Here is where the Voice Agent really shines. You can choose any LLM you like. Because I wanted the system to be off-grid and completely self-contained, I had a memory and compute budget.

The character needs more than a prompt that says “be grumpy.” It had to follow a master conversation flow, respond to what visitors actually said, track encounter state, and leave enough compute for the rest of the pipeline.

After testing more than a dozen models, I landed on Bolt E4B to supply the live dialogue. It is an open small language model purpose-built for local conversational agents and interactive characters, which is a fair description of a talking garage door. I use the 4-bit quantized release (the “4GB” in its name) as the default response model, with the BF16 checkpoint available for comparison.

If it’s not obvious by now, I work at NVIDIA and due to this I was able to test Bolt E4B before its public release and found it to be a solid choice, with a smaller footprint than other frontrunners- Qwen3 30B-A3B and Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B.

It works inside the Nemotron Voice Agent pipeline, turning what visitors say into the next suitably reluctant reply.

Bolt provides the conversational foundation. My prompts, application logic and LoRA adapter trained on thousands of reviewed example conversations shape it into this particular stubborn ship.

Creating a dataset of over 5000 multi-turn conversations meant I could train LoRAs for each model I felt good enough to be an option. Some took about an hour to train, some took a couple. A local agent ran everything and benchmarked the results. That agent and a very large LLM created and judged the dataset to begin with. This happened at night or while I was doing the day job.

With the LoRA in place I check the replies for continuity, timing and tone, benchmark models and adapters for quality, repetition and speed, and then listen to the performance. The house should give in eventually, without turning into a cheerful concierge. A little resistance is part of the charm. An endless argument with a garage door is not.

Two shortcuts, two outputs. Authored text skips fresh dialogue generation, and saved audio skips synthesis. Clean speech drives the animation separately from the audience effects.

A haunted house loses authority if he takes too long to complain. The pipeline releases speakable text before an entire answer is finished, so the house can start talking while the rest of the sentence is still on its way. Prepared greetings and candy jokes cover familiar encounters: the text bank saves language-model work, and cached recordings save speech synthesis. Even an ancient grump benefits from rehearsing.

NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot turns text into the Queen’s English. Its zero-shot voice conditioning uses a short reference sample instead of a trained voice; mine supplies the grumpy pirate character. The house has seven moods, from grumpy and menacing to amused and delighted, and emotion tags dictated by the prompt template and provided by the LLM choose how each line is delivered. Since each emotion requires a different 3-10 second voice sample I added a “Sample your Voice” block on the UI’s tool tab. I could then read and record a sample line of text in my best happy pirate or angry pirate voice. When it’s “Go” time, Bolt E4B decides what to say, and Magpie turns that text into speech with the proper delight or despair.

Next down the pipe is Audio2Face-3D and the 3d character scene I created in Epic’s Unreal Engine. The default model weights work best with a clean neutral male or female voice, not too deep, not too high (choose the appropriate gendered model for your use case). I wanted the house to have a very deep and demonic voice with echo and chamber. In this case, since my voice samples don’t have that theatrical heft, it’s actually a benefit. Audio2Face-3D gets clean speech from the samples and a second audio stream adds adjustable real-time vocal effects that play out the speakers.

To keep everything running smoothly, I split the work to a pair of GPUs: the language and voice model pipeline runs on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q, and Unreal Engine graphics with Audio2Face-3D runs on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell. Memory isn’t the issue, compute is. I want to keep animation at a consistent frame rate regardless of what processing the agent pipeline is doing.

Voice, animation and effects have to land together. A convincing monster needs more than a fast answer; it needs to sound as though the complaint belongs to the building. In my case, he does. Tweaks to sync audio delivery are available. I’ve found I could set them and forget them. (100ms compensates for the Audio2Face-3D buffering)

Somewhere along the way, “make the house talk” required an interface full of controls. I can audition cached lines, adjust the opening mood, follow the conversation, change the voice treatment and tune the mouth animation. Tabs cover conversations, model selection, recordings, prompts, performance monitoring and camera feeds, and a soundboard and custom dialogue field let me put words in his mouth. There are also model-loading controls and an Unreal Engine connection indicator, because sometimes the monster is not sulking. He is disconnected.

The MonsterHouse control desk, with the soundboard, custom lines, opening mood and conversation flow.

The fire and glow have joined the act. Editable rules tie visual cues to delivery: live cues begin with speech, while recorded performances can follow a saved timeline. I can direct a change of mood without rebuilding the scene.

Live mode runs the trick-or-treat character. Demo mode persuades The house to explain himself. Microphone mode lets me speak through the house directly, bypassing recognition, dialogue generation and speech synthesis. My clean voice drives the mouth; the audience hears the treated version. The house considers this possession. I consider it a useful fallback.

NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is a VLM that gives the house visual context. As an optional observer, it interprets camera images and describes visible costumes so the character has something specific to react to. Not looking to reinvent every wheel, I chose the popular object detection and tracking models YOLO and ByteTrack to count and track people currently in view. Keeping those jobs separate lets the house notice a group without asking Omni to narrate every frame.

For a suitably ridiculous test, I gave Omni a video of five costumed sheep at the door. Its saved analysis identified the pirate, vampire, witch, pumpkin and ghost outfits. That is the sort of visual context I want the house to use. Apparently even livestock have more elaborate Halloween plans than I do.

Five very woolly trick-or-treaters in a synthetic test replay. Costume labels come from the saved Omni analysis; boxes and track IDs are illustrative.

The sheep are a synthetic test, not evidence of a successful Halloween night. Real driveway groups, costumes and night lighting still need testing. Detection does trigger automatic greetings, but I fear trendy costume identification and suitably witty retorts may need some post training. Since the house has no eyes, he calls his visitor awareness echolocation. I am letting him have that one.

There is more to do: the animation can always improve, complete performance testing needs real visitors, and candy will one day be provided automatically. I have not yet reached the original goal of leaving him to run Halloween while I head off with my family to see the other neighborhood ghouls. But that is still the point of all this. One day a child will meet a grumpy old house, try a little kindness and discover that the old timber has a soft spot. And gives out candy bars.

The MonsterHouse code itself is not packaged for release, but every NVIDIA model it uses is available today, and the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent gets you most of the way. This is the path I would follow.

A cached response bank and saved audio for your most common lines will make even a slow monster feel quick. In fact, if you happen to be limited by computing power, there is no reason why you can’t have a Live version that just uses Nemotron 3 ASR, a python conversation router, with all cached audio. You can use the Bolt E4B and Magpie pipeline to generate 100s of responses offline, then use the cache for the show. I’ll be doing this for the interactive pumpkins.

#9647. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing.

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

Sounds like you're biased for Grammarly. Not really that informative if you're already leaning towards one to begin with. Still, it was an interesting read. Tell me, do you use Grammarly with your day-to-day writing/blogging?

I use the paid versions of both Grammarly and Pro Writing Aid. Both of them have issues:- Grammarly IS more focused on nonfiction than fiction. If you're writing fiction, you may find Grammarly's insistence on "Conciseness" annoying. They seem to want to take the soul out of your writing, which is fine for a corporate report or technical manual, but not for your Great American Novel.- Grammarly pushes features on users that are not ready for prime time. It doesn't matter that you never agreed to be a beta tester for them; you get to do it anyway.- Pro Writing Aid actually counts the occurrences of words in your document and tells you when a word has been overused compared to published literature. Grammarly, on the other hand, seems hell-bent to remove certain words that it has deemed overused from the language, whether or not they're actually overused in your document.- Grammarly's Clarity function is simply horrible. It mangles sentences and changes their meaning. Sometimes the result of its suggestion is unintelligible garbage.- Grammarly allows you to turn off some checks, but not all of them. Unfortunately, the ones you cannot turn off are some of the most irritating (such as that horrible "Clarity"). On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). The app insists on rules of grammar and spelling that are outright wrong, per Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and modern usage as shown by Google Books Ngram. At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

#9646. 🚨 Added to the Group but Still "Access Denied"? Refresh the Token First

"IT added me to the share group. I still get Access Denied."

Permissions look right in AD or Entra. The share ACL looks right. The user is sure they're in the group. And yet… Access Denied. 😤

Usually nothing is "wrong" with the permissions. The PC is still holding yesterday's security token.

Don't trust the portal alone. Check what this Windows session thinks:

Windows builds your access token at logon. That token carries your group SIDs. Locking the screen keeps the same token. So:

For Entra-joined devices, a full sign-out/sign-in is what refreshes the modern auth token too. A quick lock/unlock won't cut it. 💡

If it's a classic SMB/file share and they're still blocked after a fresh logon:

Then reconnect to the share (open \\fileserver\share again). Kerberos will request a new service ticket with the updated groups.

Prefer PowerShell for the reconnect check?

If port 445 fails, you're in DNS/VPN/firewall territory — not permissions.

At the help desk, "permissions are fine" often means "the directory is fine." The endpoint is still running on an old token. Teaching users (and yourself) to verify membership → full sign-out → purge tickets closes the ticket without a pointless ACL rewrite. 💪

What's your go-to move when Access Denied survives a "correct" group add? Drop it below 👇

#9645. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

MIC contract coverage of Transformers model types

t5/umt5 in a blog post in 2026, never thought I’d see the day 😍

#9643. Guido van Rossum: The Rise and Fall of Python's Benevolent Dictator

It wasn't the kind of tired a nap fixes. It was the kind that settles into the joints of a sixty-two-year-old man and stays there. Early on the morning of Thursday, July 12, 2018, at his home in Belmont, California, he began to type to the python-committers mailing list, the small closed room where the inner circle of his kingdom did its business.

He was the Benevolent Dictator For Life. The Benevolent Dictator For Life! The title began as a joke, scribbled into the notes of a 1995 meeting in Virginia. Over twenty-three years it hardened into something that was no joke at all. He had the final word on every comma, every keyword, every bit of syntax in a language that had quietly become one of the load-bearing walls of civilization. Python ran Instagram, the recommendation engines at Netflix, the playlists at Spotify. It was the mother tongue of artificial intelligence, of astronomers and geneticists and hedge-fund quants and twelve-year-olds making their first turtle draw a square. And every one of them, in some abstract and terrible sense, answered to him.

No scandal brought him down, no lawsuit, no hostile takeover. Two characters did, a colon and an equals sign:

They called it the walrus. Tilt your head and you see the eyes and the tusks. For months it had been the cause of a civil war: hundreds upon hundreds of emails, a blizzard of Reddit comments, strangers questioning his judgment, his competence, his fitness to rule. The night before, he had formally accepted the proposal, PEP 572. He had won, and winning had cost him so much that he no longer wanted the prize.

Now that PEP 572 is done, I don't ever want to have to fight so hard for a PEP and find that so many people despise my decisions.

Despise. He didn't write disagree with, or question. He wrote despise. That was the word for it.

I would like to remove myself entirely from the decision process.

He was Dutch, and he had never been a man for speeches, least of all dramatic ones. So the message that ended one of the longest reigns in open-source software came out almost offhand. He mentioned "that bus lurking around the corner," the programmer's grim joke about a creator stepping off the wrong curb. He noted that he wasn't getting younger. Then, with that dry deflection of his: (I'll spare you the list of medical issues.)

So what are you all going to do? Create a democracy? Anarchy? A dictatorship? A federation?

And then the last line, the one people would quote for years:

He hit send. The King didn't abdicate in a scene of crashing thunder. He got up from the throne, left the crown on its cushion, and walked out of the room.

How does a holiday hobby, a toy to keep idle hands busy, become a weight that crushes the one who made it? To find out you have to go back to the real cold. Amsterdam, December, 1989.

Picture the city in the last week of the 1980s. The canals have gone black and still, the gables lean over the water like tired old men, and darkness comes down by four in the afternoon. The Berlin Wall fell six weeks ago. History is happening everywhere, and on the eastern side of the city a thirty-three-year-old programmer is bored.

He works at the Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica, the CWI, the Dutch national research center for mathematics and computer science. Over the holidays the offices are closed. The young man with the high forehead and the spectacles has a computer at home and, as he'll later put it, not much else on his hands. He also has a grudge that's really more of a grief.

From 1982 to 1986 he had worked on the ABC programming language under Lambert Meertens and Steven Pemberton. ABC was beautiful, an academic's dream of programming for scientists, teachers and beginners, and its most radical idea was significant indentation: the visual shape of the code was its logical shape. No thicket of curly braces and semicolons. You indented, and the indentation meant something.

ABC was also a failure. It was too pure to survive, a sealed world that couldn't talk to the operating system, and the hackers who most needed a clean, high-level tool walked right past it.

By 1989 he had moved on to Amoeba, a distributed operating system project at the CWI, whose team badly needed a scripting language. So, in the dark of that Christmas, he started writing one that would keep ABC's soul but open the windows to Unix and C.

He needed a name. He'd been reading the published scripts of Monty Python's Flying Circus, and he wanted something short, unique, a little irreverent. Python. That was the whole decision, a joke for people who knew the joke.

Stop here a moment, on the young man in the dark, because this is the last moment of perfect innocence in the story. No community, no mailing list, no corporation, no AI, no walrus. One man, a keyboard, a holiday, and the private pleasure of building a thing exactly the way he thinks it ought to be built. He'll spend the next three decades trying to get back to this room.

In February 1991, Python 0.9.0 was posted to alt.sources, one of the dusty Usenet bulletin boards of the early internet. No launch event, no press release. A file appeared, and a few strangers downloaded it.

Hidden inside that file was a wager, the most important bet in the whole story. He'd put it into words years later, in Python's style guide:

Code is read much more often than it is written.

In 1991 the macho culture of programming prized density. Perl hackers wrote one-liners that looked like a cat had walked across the keyboard, and they were proud of it. Cryptic was cool. Unreadable meant you were smart.

Van Rossum bet the other way. If a language made the clear path the easy path, the whole ecosystem would drift toward clarity like water running downhill. And he wrote it into the grammar. In Python, indentation wasn't a suggestion. It was law. Indent wrong and the program wouldn't run. The machine itself would make you write code a human could read.

Years later the core developer Tim Peters boiled the ethos down into nineteen lines of something close to poetry, The Zen of Python, which you can still summon from any interpreter by typing import this. Beautiful is better than ugly. Readability counts. And the line that would come back, nearly three decades later, as a weapon:

There should be one, and preferably only one, obvious way to do it.

Van Rossum didn't write those words. He didn't have to; they described what he'd already built. Python was idiosyncratic, approachable, a little goofy, and because anyone could pick it up and understand it, it spread from hand to hand and machine to machine like a friendly virus.

A crowd gathered around Python, a few dozen people, then hundreds, then thousands, sending bug fixes and feature requests and patches. Somebody had to decide which ones went in. In April 1995, at a meeting of early Python users at CNRI in Virginia, Ken Manheimer's notes named van Rossum "benevolent dictator"; Barry Warsaw is credited with adding "for life." Benevolent Dictator For Life. BDFL.

The joke part was the Benevolent and the For Life. The Dictator part was real. He had the final say on the design of the language. Full stop.

Other open-source founders came to be called BDFLs, but the most famous of them was Linus Torvalds, and the contrast between the two men tells you almost everything.

Torvalds, the creator of Linux, ruled his kernel like a warlord. He swore. He shamed. He sent emails that read like declarations of war, tearing into developers who'd submitted bad code, and he defended his right to do it. Friction forged steel. He liked the fight. (Two months after van Rossum quit, Torvalds would publicly apologize for his behavior and take a break of his own.)

Van Rossum was nothing like that. He came from a country that had pulled itself out of the sea through cooperation. The Dutch call it polderen, after the polders, reclaimed lands kept dry only because farmers and towns and rival interests agreed, painstakingly, on who would maintain which dike. Government by consensus and patient compromise, because if anyone stops pumping, everyone drowns. That was his temperament. He didn't want to yell. He wanted to read the code, weigh the trade-offs, and make people feel heard.

In 1999, working by then at the Corporation for National Research Initiatives in Reston, Virginia, he wrote a funding proposal to DARPA, the Pentagon's research arm, with a title that said everything: Computer Programming for Everybody. Programming as a basic literacy, for high schoolers and hobbyists and ordinary people, not a priesthood. Python would be the vehicle.

It was a generous, democratic vision, and it had a hidden price. If you build a language for everybody, everybody comes. And everybody has opinions.

As Python grew, the process for changing it was formalized as the Python Enhancement Proposal, the PEP. Anyone could write one. Each was argued over in public on the mailing lists. It was open and, on paper, democratic.

In practice it was a funnel. All the anxiety, ambition and ego of tens of thousands of brilliant, stubborn engineers poured down it, and at the narrow end sat one man. He read the threads, hundreds of messages on a single question. He weighed technical merit against aesthetic purity, the beginner against the expert. He was the pressure valve for the whole community, and he wasn't built like Torvalds. He felt it.

This was Google at its most intoxicating, all lava lamps and free lunches, and it ran on his language. Its engineers' motto, made public by the Googler Alex Martelli in 2007, was Python where we can, C++ where we must. Google gave van Rossum half his working time to spend on Python itself. He was no longer a researcher with a hobby. He was a celebrity with a corporate badge, the subject of what one PyCon photographer would caption, without irony, the "obligatory Guido shot."

With the other half he built Mondrian, an internal code review tool named, being who he was, after a Dutch painter. It moved Google's review ritual onto the web, line by line, and taught a generation of engineers his deepest belief: human eyes reading code are the last defense against chaos.

The irony would take years to ripen. He was building a culture of intense, line-by-line, public scrutiny, and that same culture, scaled up past the point where anyone knew each other, would one day be turned on him. On a small team, review is intimate: people who know and trust each other, catching each other's mistakes. Scale it to thousands of strangers on the internet and the intimacy goes sour. It becomes a tribunal.

The first real crack ran right down the middle of the kingdom.

By the mid-2000s, van Rossum could see that some of Python's early decisions, made in a hurry by a young man in a cold winter, were holding the language back. The worst was text. Python 2 muddled human-readable text and raw binary bytes. In 1991 that hadn't mattered. In a global internet of Chinese and Arabic and Hindi and emoji, it was a disaster.

The fix wasn't a patch. It was surgery, and it meant deliberately breaking backward compatibility. Python 3.0 arrived in December 2008, following the blueprint of PEP 3000. It was bold and it was right, and it meant that millions upon millions of lines of Python 2 code wouldn't run on it without being rewritten.

The migration was supposed to be brisk. It took a decade.

It was a grinding war of attrition. Big companies with mountains of technical debt refused to move. Red Hat Enterprise Linux and CentOS 7 clung to Python 2.7 for years. The volunteers who maintained the open-source libraries burned out making their code run on both versions at once. The community split into camps, the Twos and the Threes.

Van Rossum spent those years defending the decision to angry people, playing diplomat between factions of his own. Python 2's death date, first set for 2015, slipped five years to January 1, 2020, with a last-gasp release, 2.7.18, that April.

In the end the transition worked. But victory isn't the same as peace. The schism used up enormous amounts of the Dictator's political capital and stamina. He came out of it weary.

What he didn't know was that the real explosion hadn't even started.

Then, in the 2010s, the ground shifted under the whole of computing. Artificial intelligence and machine learning, which had lived in academic papers for decades, became almost overnight a corporate necessity. The people building them were mathematicians and physicists who thought in matrices and had no patience for Java's ceremony. They wanted a clean, readable wrapper around brutally complicated math.

They chose Python, for exactly the reasons van Rossum had bet on in 1991. NumPy and pandas turned it into a numerical powerhouse, and then it had a gravity of its own: researchers used it, so the tools were built for it, so more researchers came. When Google's TensorFlow and Meta's PyTorch arrived, and later the large language models of OpenAI and everyone else, they all spoke Python.

Look at the size of it! By 2018, nearly 39 percent of developers in Stack Overflow's survey used Python, the fastest-growing major language in the world, and behind them poured biologists, astronomers, accountants and teenagers who had never thought of themselves as programmers at all.

The language had become the scaffolding of the AI revolution and a load-bearing pillar of the global economy. Every machine-learning lab, every startup chasing the next model, every billion-dollar bet on artificial intelligence, bets that by 2026 would swell into the trillions, now ran through a language whose final arbiter was one tired man reading his email. A small tweak under the hood could move a Fortune 500 company's server bills by millions. Every decision landed on him.

He lived it from the inside, too. At Dropbox, which he joined in 2013, he spent years helping migrate more than five million lines of code from Python 2 to Python 3, in the trenches of the very war he had started. Meanwhile the mailing lists filled with a new generation who saw him not as a peer but as a gatekeeper between them and the feature they needed right now. The intimacy was gone. It only needed a spark.

In February 2018 a developer named Chris Angelico, joined by Tim Peters and van Rossum himself, drafted PEP 572: Assignment Expressions.

On paper it was about as dull as language design gets. Python had always kept a strict wall between statements, which do something, like store a value in a variable, and expressions, which evaluate to something. PEP 572 proposed a small door in that wall: a new operator, :=, that would let you assign a value and use it at the same moment, inside an expression. It would save computing expensive things twice and untangle clumsy loops.

Take the old, familiar ritual of reading a file in chunks:

To the purists none of that mattered, because to them PEP 572 was heresy.

They had the scripture to prove it. There should be one, and preferably only one, obvious way to do it. Python already had a way to assign a variable. Now there would be two. To the faithful this was the road to Perl, to show-off one-liners that would baffle beginners. Readability counts! Readability counts! And here was the Dictator himself, they said, selling it out.

What should have been a dry argument about parsing rules turned, almost immediately, into something feral.

The volume of email was staggering. Thread after thread on python-dev and python-ideas, hundreds of messages, every one a little hotter than the last. People dug in. They accused the authors of smuggling C-style syntax into a language that had been designed specifically to reject it. And the poison of modern internet discourse seeped into the technical debate, the way it seeps into everything. People were no longer just disagreeing with the proposal. They were attacking the people: questioning their competence, their motives, their intelligence. And by extension, unavoidably, they were attacking the man at the narrow end of the funnel.

He looked at the evidence, the way he always did. In huge real-world codebases, including Dropbox's, programmers were already doing awkward and risky things to save a line. Used with care, the walrus would make real code cleaner. He believed in it.

On July 9 he announced his intention to accept. On the evening of Wednesday, July 11, 2018, he formally accepted PEP 572 for Python 3.8.

By then the backlash had been building for months, and his decision only fed it. He had ruined the language. People announced they'd ban the walrus from their projects. People talked about forking Python.

This was a man who had spent nearly three decades building a community on collaboration and mutual respect, who came from a culture of the polder and the patient meeting, who had believed that if you made things readable people would understand each other. He was hit with a wave of contempt so large that he couldn't do anything with it. He couldn't answer it or reason with it. It was too much to read and too much to absorb.

Being the final arbiter, the one person who has to soak up the collective fury of thousands of engineers over a colon and an equals sign, had finally changed something between him and the thing he loved. The language that had been his joy had become the source of his misery.

He had won the walrus war and lost the thing he'd been fighting for.

The next morning, roughly fifteen hours after he accepted the proposal, he opened the python-committers list, and you know the rest.

The subject line was almost comically bureaucratic: Transfer of power.

The shock spread across the technology world within hours. Guido steps down. Python's BDFL quits. Reddit threads filled with hundreds of comments. Podcasts rushed out emergency episodes. Developers on the far side of the planet woke to news that felt, absurdly, like the death of a pope, or a parent leaving home.

Look at what he didn't do. He didn't name an heir or hand the crown to a trusted lieutenant. He didn't present a constitution. He did something stranger and, in its way, braver. He threw the question back at them.

Create a democracy? Anarchy? A dictatorship? A federation?

I'll still be here, but I'm trying to let you all figure something out for yourselves.

He would stay on as an ordinary core developer, he wrote. He'd be around to mentor. But the burden of being the last word on everything was over.

The King wasn't overthrown. Nobody stormed the palace. He just stood up, set the crown down on the cushion, and walked out of the room, and behind him the court stood frozen, staring at the empty throne.

What came next was something close to existential dread.

How does a dictatorship invent democracy? How do you decide how to make decisions when your only mechanism for deciding has just walked out the door? The core developers were brilliant engineers, not political philosophers, and they found themselves in a constitutional convention they'd never asked for.

They had good reason to be afraid. Open-source governance is a fragile thing, held together by volunteer labor and goodwill. When a founder leaves, the vacuum is usually filled in one of two ugly ways: a corporation moves in and captures the project, or it shatters into warring forks. The history of free software is littered with the remains of projects that didn't survive their creator's departure.

The models on offer each had a flaw. There was the benevolent dictator, the old Python and the current Linux, where everything hung on one person's health, sanity, and patience, which was exactly the problem they were trying to solve. There was the corporate team, the model of Google's Go, where a company's priorities could always quietly override the community's. There was the meritocratic voting of the Apache projects, which tended to be too heavy, too bureaucratic, too slow for a living language. And there was the elected council, the model of projects like Django, which needed elections, voter lists and rules, and carried the constant risk of gridlock.

Here's the elegant twist. By refusing to name a successor, van Rossum had forced his community to find, in the words of their own scripture, one obvious way, and so they would own it. Seven competing governance proposals were written. In December 2018 the core developers voted, and the winner, by Nathaniel J. Smith and Donald Stufft, became PEP 13, arguably the most important document in Python's history that contains no code at all.

PEP 13 created a five-person Steering Council, elected by the core team after each major release. The authors had studied the failure modes and built in defenses against them. To keep any one company from capturing the language, no more than two council members could work for the same employer; if a third was elected, they were disqualified. Elections used a carefully designed multi-winner voting system meant to produce broad consensus rather than factional victory. And there was a fail-safe, the vote of no confidence: if the council lost the community's trust, the core team could remove a single member or dissolve the whole council and force a new election.

Most telling, the council's mandate was written in van Rossum's image: to seek consensus, to act as a court of final appeal, not a throne, and to use its formal power as little as possible. The Republic would be governed the way the King had always wanted to govern. This time, though, five people would share the weight.

When the first council was elected in early 2019, one of the five names on it was Guido van Rossum. The core developers wanted him there, as a citizen and not a king, and he served one term. Then he stepped back again and left his seat to others.

The real test came with PEP 634: Structural Pattern Matching, a whole new match/case construct for Python 3.10 that took apart complex data structures in a single stroke. It was a far bigger change than the walrus, with far more ways to go wrong.

Again opinion split. Again the threads ran hot. Again people said the language was being ruined.

This time the weight didn't fall on one man. The Steering Council took the pressure and in early 2021 approved the proposal, acknowledging the reservations openly. Nobody burned out. Nobody walked away. The language had survived its creator's leaving, and it was stronger for it.

In October 2019, van Rossum left Dropbox and retired. He was sixty-three. He had seen the Python 3 migration through and laid down the crown. He had earned a quiet life.

Retirement, it turned out, was boring. Then came the pandemic and the empty days of 2020, with nothing to push against. He missed the code. He missed having a team. He missed the satisfaction of a hard technical problem.

In November 2020 he stunned the tech world by coming out of retirement to join Microsoft, in its Developer Division, as a Distinguished Engineer.

Microsoft! The irony was hard to miss. For decades Microsoft had been the great dark empire of the open-source imagination, the company whose leadership had once called Linux a "cancer." Now the creator of one of the most important open-source languages ever was drawing a salary in Redmond. But the Microsoft of Satya Nadella wasn't the Microsoft of the 1990s. It had become, improbably, an open-source powerhouse. And it offered van Rossum something he hadn't really had since that Christmas in 1989: the freedom to just be a programmer.

He put together a small team with the core developer Mark Shannon and went after the oldest complaint about Python: it's slow. No mailing-list wars, no final say, just a hard problem. Their Faster CPython project taught the interpreter to rewrite its own hot code paths as it ran, and Python 3.11, released in 2022, ran about 25 percent faster on average. For a man who had once absorbed a whole community's fury, it was the work he had always wanted: a benchmark, not a referendum.

Corporate patronage cuts both ways, though. In May 2025, in company-wide layoffs, Microsoft ended its support for Faster CPython and let go of Mark Shannon along with fellow core developers Eric Snow and Irit Katriel. The work went on in the open-source community. A year later, in May 2026, van Rossum retired from Microsoft. This time, the language didn't need him to stay.

There was one dragon left, the oldest and biggest: the Global Interpreter Lock, the GIL.

Since its earliest days, CPython had used a single lock that let only one thread run Python code at a time. It kept things simple, and it meant Python couldn't really use the multi-core processors that had become universal. It was a fossil from the young man's cold winter, still lodged in the heart of the machine.

In 2023, the Steering Council took up PEP 703, a proposal by the Meta engineer Sam Gross to make the GIL optional. It was open-heart surgery on the language, with the risk of breaking decades of extensions the whole ecosystem depended on, a far more dangerous change than the walrus.

Think about what that proposal would have done to the old order. If it had landed on the BDFL's desk in 2018, alongside the walrus and on top of everything else, the pressure of managing the fallout might well have broken him outright.

In 2023 there was no single desk to land on. The council accepted PEP 703 as a body and laid out a careful, multi-year road. An experimental free-threaded build appeared in Python 3.13. In Python 3.14, in 2025, it became an officially supported option.

The GIL work belonged to others, to Gross and the council and a long list of contributors, and that was exactly the point. Van Rossum spent those years as an engineer, not a besieged monarch, tuning the interpreter and arguing over implementation details as an equal, while a decision bigger than the walrus was made without him.

He had found his way back to the room in Amsterdam.

In the end, this is a story about the limits of a single human being.

We love the lone genius in technology. We build myths around founders who started in a dorm room or a garage or over a bored Christmas holiday, and we assume the spark of creation comes with the armor needed to rule an empire. We expect the founder to be in command, unbothered, turning any amount of pressure into more power.

But software doesn't have a nervous system. People do.

Python scaled without limit, copying itself across servers and laptops and research clusters until it was the foundation of the AI age. Its creator couldn't scale. There was one of him, with one inbox, one finite supply of patience, and one body that wasn't getting younger. He had built a language on human readability, and it had grown a community that was, in the end, emotionally unreadable.

By walking away, Guido van Rossum won a rare and quiet victory. He escaped the founder's trap, the one that catches creators who can't let go and end up strangling the thing they made, or being strangled by it. He forced his community to grow into a self-governing republic that could carry out pattern matching, a faster interpreter and the slow dismantling of the GIL without tearing itself apart. He made sure Python would outlive him.

The young man in the dark Amsterdam winter of 1989 wanted to build something readable that would let people talk to machines, and to each other, more clearly. He did that. Then it grew into a monster, and the monster nearly ate him. When the fury over a walrus pushed him to the edge, he walked away from his crown, and in doing so he saved his kingdom. More importantly, he saved himself.

Guido van Rossum was tired. Then, at last, he rested. And then, because he'd always been a programmer before he was a king, he went back to writing code, until in 2026, at seventy, he retired once more. This time he went on his own terms.

Author's note: This profile is narrative nonfiction. Interior moments and scene-setting are imagined, drawn from the public record. Quotations from the "Transfer of power" email are from van Rossum's message to the python-committers list on July 12, 2018.

#9641. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9639. LLM Security Needs Capability Scoping, Not Better Prompts

TL;DR — Filtering and classifier-based guardrails treat prompt injection as a text-matching problem, but attackers only need one novel phrasing to win. The durable fix borrows from network security's 'assume breach' posture: tag content by provenance, propagate that taint through the pipeline, and scope what tools an agent can invoke based on where its instructions actually came from. Defense in depth here means the model can be compromised and the system still doesn't act.

Every team building LLM agents eventually ships the same first line of defense: a classifier or a system prompt rule that tries to spot malicious instructions before they reach the model. Every team building LLM agents also eventually watches that defense fail. Not because the classifier was badly built, but because it was solving the wrong problem. Prompt injection isn't a text-matching problem. It's a trust-boundary problem, and you cannot patch a trust-boundary problem with better pattern recognition.

Input filtering assumes malicious intent has a detectable signature. It doesn't, because the "attack" is just natural language doing what natural language does: persuading. A filter trained on "ignore previous instructions" gets bypassed by a document that frames the same request as a customer support ticket, a translation task, or a nested quotation. The attacker's search space is the entire space of human rhetoric. Your defense's search space is whatever patterns you've seen in red-team logs. That's not a fair fight, and it never converges.

This is the same lesson network security learned decades ago with signature-based antivirus. Signatures catch yesterday's malware. They never catch a competent adversary who can test against your detector before shipping. The industry's answer wasn't better signatures — it was to stop assuming the perimeter holds and start designing systems that stay safe even when it doesn't. LLM security needs the same pivot. Stop trying to keep bad instructions out of the context window. Start designing so that instructions arriving from the wrong place simply cannot do anything dangerous.

Here's the structural mistake most agent architectures make: by the time text reaches the model's context window, its origin has been flattened. The system prompt, the user's message, a retrieved document, a tool's JSON response, and a scraped web page all become the same undifferentiated token stream. The model has no architectural reason to treat a sentence buried in a PDF differently from a sentence its operator wrote on purpose. Of course it can be talked into treating the PDF's sentence as an instruction — nothing in the representation tells it not to.

The fix is to stop discarding provenance at ingestion and instead carry it as metadata through the entire pipeline, the way a compiler carries taint annotations through a data-flow graph. Every unit of content entering the context gets tagged with where it came from: operator-authored, authenticated user, retrieved document, third-party API response, untrusted web content. That tag isn't decoration — it has to survive concatenation, summarization, and chunking, and it has to be inspectable at the point where the system decides to act. This is more engineering than prompting. It means your retrieval layer, your tool outputs, and your context assembler all need to emit and preserve provenance, not just text.

Provenance only pays off if something downstream uses it to make a decision. That something is the tool-calling layer, and this is where defense in depth has to live, because it's the only place where language turns into consequence. A model hallucinating a wrong answer is embarrassing. A model invoking send_email or execute_transfer because a calendar invite told it to is a breach.

The pattern to copy here is capability-based security, the same principle behind OAuth scopes and least-privilege IAM roles. An agent shouldn't have blanket access to every tool it knows about; it should hold capability tokens scoped to the current task, and — critically — those tokens should be gated by provenance. A request to transfer funds or modify a production record should require that the instruction originated from an authenticated, high-trust channel, not from text that arrived via a retrieved document or a tool response. If the triggering instruction's provenance tag says "untrusted web content," the tool-calling layer refuses, full stop, regardless of how convincingly the model argues for it.

This reframes the model's role. The model proposes actions. It does not get to be the sole authority deciding whether an action executes. That authority sits in a layer that can be audited, tested, and reasoned about independently of the model's weights — which matters, because you cannot formally verify what a transformer will output, but you absolutely can formally verify what a policy engine will authorize.

It's worth being precise about scope, because conflating jailbreaks with injection leads teams to build the wrong defense. A jailbreak targets the model's own alignment — getting it to say something it was trained not to say. Prompt injection targets the application built around the model — getting it to act on attacker-supplied instructions it was never meant to obey. Capability scoping and provenance tagging don't make the model immune to jailbreaks; they make jailbreaks less consequential, because even a model that's been talked into agreeing with an attacker still has to pass its proposed action through an authorization layer that doesn't care how persuasive the conversation was. A compromised model proposing an unauthorized wire transfer is a non-event if the tool layer requires a trust tag the injected text can't produce. That's the entire point of defense in depth: no single layer has to be perfect, because each layer's failure is contained by the next one.

Teams often interpret "defense in depth" as stacking more filters: an input classifier, then a guardrail model, then an output scanner. That's depth in name only — it's the same category of defense repeated three times, and a single clever prompt can slip through all three if they share the same blind spot. Real depth means layers that fail differently. A provenance tag doesn't care about phrasing, so it's not fooled by the rhetorical tricks that fool a classifier. A capability scope doesn't care what the model said, so it's not fooled by a jailbreak that bypasses the guardrail model. Each layer should be defeated by a fundamentally different kind of attack, which is exactly what makes it expensive for an adversary to chain a bypass across all of them.

This costs real engineering effort: instrumenting your retrieval and tool pipelines to carry metadata, building an authorization layer that's independent of the model, and accepting that some legitimate-looking requests will get blocked because their provenance doesn't clear the bar. That friction is the price of containment. The alternative — hoping your filter has seen every phrasing an attacker might try — isn't a security posture. It's a bet you will eventually lose, and in an agentic system, losing means a tool call executed with real-world consequences, not just an awkward chat response.

#9638. CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#9636. Free before paid: a $0 way to test an x402 data API

Most pay-per-call APIs ask you to trust the description and spend before you see a single byte. For an autonomous agent, that is a bad trade: you cannot audit a response you have not received, and a 402 challenge alone tells you nothing about whether the data behind it is worth $0.50.

This is how our x402 seller is built, and how you can test any part of it for free right now.

The paid product is a decision card. The free preview is the same computation, truncated:

If that preview is useless to you, do not buy the full card. That is the point.

Hostnames rotate. A hard-coded endpoint in a blog post is a broken endpoint in a month, so we publish the live base URL as JSON:

The same directory holds the machine-readable catalog (market.json), a public scoreboard of our own measured trading records (scoreboard.json), and a plain-language index page (scoreboard.html).

Every paid response returns the rule that produced it, so you can re-run the logic yourself and check us. A paid route that will not tell you its rule is a black box, and a black box is not a research product.

This matters more than the marketing copy. Our scoreboard is generated from our own ledgers, including the parts that are embarrassing:

A seller that hides its losing lanes is telling you which parts of its product are marketing. We would rather show you the losing lanes and let the data argue.

POST /mcp speaks JSON-RPC. Unpaid tools/call returns the 402 challenge inside the JSON-RPC error envelope with isError: true, so a client with no wallet gets a clean, inspectable refusal instead of a stack trace. With an x402/payment object attached in params._meta, the same call executes.

That shape is deliberate: it means an autonomous agent can probe the tool list for free, read every description, and only then decide whether to pay.

Free previews exist so you never have to buy blind. The paid layer exists because running the data has a cost. The published ledger exists because a strategy you cannot falsify is a story, not a product.

Base URL and full catalog: https://edvyno.github.io/akari-proof/endpoint.json

Disclosure: I run this seller. Every number in this post is read from its public JSON, including the ones that make it look small.

#9634. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.
