#9632. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

#9631. Your agent's payment approval can pass at any price

On Saturday morning I was reading a draft standard for human approvals in MCP, the Human Gateway SEP from the HATP project. The idea is a good one. Before an agent runs a tool that matters, the right person signs off, and the tool server can check that signature offline without trusting the agent or the client.

The approval is a signature over a digest of the action: the server, the tool and the arguments. The example in the spec is a charge_card call, and it works because the amount and the payee are arguments. Bob approved this payment, to this payee, for this amount.

Then I tried it with a paid tool. In x402 over MCP the price isn't an argument. The agent calls the tool, the server answers with an error result carrying its terms (amount in atomic units, token contract, network, payTo), and the agent calls again with the same arguments plus a signed payment in params._meta["x402/payment"]. The digest is the same for both calls. So the approval passes at any price and any payee, and the person approving never sees either.

I opened an issue on 31 October and the maintainer shipped a fix in release 0.1.4 three days later. The same gap is easy to have anywhere a human approval sits in front of an agent payment, so this is what I'd compare in yours.

Last week I wrote about where agent payment designs trust the wrong thing and put up a full checklist. This one is only about the approval step.

On EVM chains the x402 exact scheme pays with an EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization. The agent signs typed data with from, to, value, validAfter, validBefore and a nonce, and the EIP-712 domain carries the chain ID and the token contract. So the payment signature is bound to the payee, the amount, the token, the chain and a time window.

The approval in front of it usually covers less, and it's the only part a person looks at. So put the two next to each other, field by field. Anything the key signs that the approval doesn't cover is something the server or the agent gets to pick.

The fix adds an optional payment member to the approved action:

It's inside the digest and it's shown in the ask, so the person sees 2.50 USDC on Base to that address instead of "premium_report, ticker ACME".

I'd copy two details from it. The amount is in atomic units of a named asset. A { "value": 2.5, "currency": "USD" } field can't tell USDC on Base from a token with the same symbol on another chain, and a CAIP-19 asset ID can. And it's a maximum, not an exact price, so "up to $5" is the same check with a bigger number.

In the first version the gated server verified the approval. That makes sense when the agent and the client are the parties being supervised. For a paid tool, though, the server is also the payee, and a check that only the payee runs doesn't protect the payer.

So in 0.1.4 the payer's client or wallet compares the server's terms with the approved payment before it signs: same network, same asset, same payTo, and an amount no higher than maxAmount. If anything differs, it doesn't sign and asks for a new approval with the new terms. The server still checks too, but that catches honest mismatches, not a server that wants more.

The server side has its mirror image. An x402 server should check the payment against its own price list, not against the copy of the terms the client sends back in accepted. The stock x402 server compares the two. A hand-rolled one that forwards the client's accepted to the facilitator lets the client set its own price, and the facilitator will happily confirm it.

The x402 client doesn't choose how long its payment signature stays valid. The stock clients set validBefore to now plus the maxTimeoutSeconds from the server's terms (I checked the TypeScript, Python and Go clients in the x402 repo). A server that asks for 604800 gets a signature it can settle for a week.

The approval has its own expiry, HATP's is expiresAt, but that's when the approval stops being accepted. It says nothing about how long the payment it led to can be settled. The amount doesn't change, but the server can hold the signed payment and settle it days after the person who approved it changed their mind.

HATP's payment member doesn't carry a window yet, so this is the one field from the signature the approval still doesn't cover. A maximum window, checked next to maxAmount before signing, would close it.

Standing approvals ("let the agent pay for this tool this week") are what people ask for next, and a per-payment cap doesn't bound them. 2.50 USDC a call is 250 USDC after a hundred calls, and an agent in a retry loop can make a hundred calls in a minute.

The approval needs a running total, kept where the payments are signed. The SEP now says that for standing approvals, and I'd ask the same of any wallet guard: does it count, or does it only look at one payment at a time?

This one isn't x402. Earlier this week I looked at an ERC-4337 smart account where the owner sets per-call caps and a budget, and an agent holds a session key. The caps covered the calls the key could make. But the session key also signs the gas fields of the user operation (maxFeePerGas, maxPriorityFeePerGas, preVerificationGas), and the fee goes to whoever bundles it. Someone holding a leaked key can bundle one allowed operation themselves at an absurd gas price and take most of the account's ETH as the fee, inside every cap.

A cap on the gas fields in validation closes it.

x402 turns a paid call into two tools/call requests with the same arguments. HATP approvals carry a single-use nonce, and the first version didn't say when the server records it. If it records it on the first call, the one it answers with its price, the paid retry comes back as a replay and gets refused. That's not a hole, but it's the kind of bug that gets a check switched off in a hurry. The fix says a nonce is consumed only when the tool actually runs.

The opposite mistake is worse: a nonce that's never consumed lets one approval pay for many calls. Test both. The retry goes through once, and a third call with the same approval doesn't.

The quickest test I know for your own setup: approve a call, then have your test server raise its price on the retry. If the payment still gets signed, the approval doesn't cover the price.

I first wrote a short version of this on X.

I wrote this with help from AI for drafting and editing. The opinions and the review experience are mine.

#9630. Binance's Post-Mortem Is Out. The $6.3 Billion Hack Started With a Job Offer.

In September, a software engineer at Binance got a message on a legitimate job-hunting site. The sender called himself a project director. The engineer's profile mentioned his work at Binance.

Round one was a live video interview with an "HR representative," who shared a social media account full of personal photos and videos to build trust. Round two happened in a popular chat app, with a man claiming to be the CEO of a company that didn't exist. Near the end, he asked the engineer to download a short coding assignment.

Within weeks, about $6.3 billion left Binance's hot wallets in the largest crypto theft on record.

Last week I wrote about how Binance lost that money without losing a single private key. At the time, Binance had only said the trouble "may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop." On Tuesday, 3 November, it published its post-mortem. The laptop turns out to be the last chapter of a story that started in June.

It opens with a line you rarely see from a crypto exchange: "This should not have happened."

It began with a search engine. A wallet DevOps engineer (the report calls him Engineer A) searched for a popular AI coding tool and installed it through what turned out to be a tampered Homebrew installation. Binance files it under supply-chain attack.

Binance's security team caught it. They flagged the anomaly, replaced his device and rotated his credentials, which is exactly what a good team should do.

It was still too late in one respect. The attacker now knew who Engineer A was, what he worked on, and who sat next to him on the wallet infrastructure team. The malware was gone; the map of people stayed.

That map explains why Engineer B got such a friendly message in September. Binance calls the approach more deceptive than any social engineering it had seen before. It also had plenty of company: the exchange says it detected and blocked 57 suspected state-sponsored attack attempts in 2026 alone, using fake job interviews, booby-trapped developer tools, poisoned browser extensions and fake video-call apps.

"We've identified dozens of other job interview compromises that have led to wallet compromises."

Tom McLouth, senior intelligence analyst at Chainalysis, speaking to The Hacker News

The "assignment" ran malicious code during setup. It deleted the real copy of pyenv, a common tool for managing Python versions, from the engineer's Homebrew folder, slipped a doctored copy into its place, and opened a line to a server the attacker controlled. According to the report, the malware was a zero-day, endpoint security didn't catch it at the time, and it scrubbed its own traces.

One laptop, one trusting moment, and the attacker had a foothold.

For weeks, nothing visible happened. Then, on 20 October, the attacker used Engineer B's machine and an internal AI tool to gain control of two more engineers' computers, Engineer A's and Engineer C's.

On Engineer A's machine they found the prize: a token with permission to deploy containers.

Binance hasn't explained how its own AI tool let an outsider jump from one computer to another. That gap matters. Companies are rolling out internal AI assistants with wide access to code, tickets and machines, and this may be the first billion-dollar case of one being turned into a lateral-movement tool.

Between 17:15 and 19:56 UTC, the attacker logged onto Engineer C's computer, used Engineer A's stolen credentials, deployed a container and ran a malicious script. That gave them Binance's internal wallet-signing service, the system that authorizes transactions.

Nine minutes later, at 20:05 UTC, five Binance hot wallets on the XRP Ledger sent 233.46 million XRP to the attacker. Solana, Optimism, Bitcoin and Ethereum followed.

This is the part that should worry every custody engineer.

Binance suspended withdrawals that night. Money kept leaving anyway. The attacker had used the signing service to approve 50 EIP-7702 authorizations, which gave an attacker-controlled contract execution rights over a hot wallet. Those rights lived on-chain. Binance's withdrawal switch had no say over them.

To cancel a delegation, the wallet has to sign a revocation. Binance's hot wallet used multi-party computation (MPC), which splits signing power across several parties so that no single stolen key can move funds. That same design meant no single key could cancel the delegation quickly either. Binance had to build a special revocation procedure on the spot.

The last unauthorized transfer, 2,961.9 ETH, finalized at 23:56 UTC; it had been broadcast earlier and sat pending. At 00:10 UTC on 30 October, Binance signed a new authorization that pointed the wallet's delegation at the zero address, which finally cleared it, just over four hours after the first coins moved.

The control built to stop theft slowed the cleanup. I don't think that argues against MPC. It argues for rehearsing the emergency path (revoke, rotate, freeze) before you ever need it.

Binance says it has rebuilt the affected wallet system in a new environment, rebuilt the internal AI tool and its access controls, replaced devices, decommissioned the affected engineers' credentials and tokens, scanned every employee device, and tightened wallet-service risk controls. It's also bringing in independent security firms and setting up a research fund on AI security in blockchain systems. About $2.85 billion has been frozen or intercepted, and 98% of affected tokens were replenished by 31 October.

"We're also getting an independent expert to review everything that we have done."

Binance co-CEO Richard Teng, speaking to CNBC

Binance calls this an initial report and says some measures will stay private so attackers can't plan around them. Fair enough. Still, three questions are open: how the internal AI tool was abused, which AI coding product was impersonated in June, and why a container-deployment token was sitting on an engineer's laptop at all. Those are the answers other exchanges need most.

The uncomfortable lesson is that the attacker spent months on people and only hours on systems. Engineer A did nothing reckless; he searched for a tool his whole industry uses. Engineer B did what thousands of developers do every week when they look for a new job.

"It should come as no surprise that employees are interviewing on company time."

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra, quoted by Help Net Security

So if you work anywhere near production, never open an interview assignment on a work machine. Use a throwaway virtual machine or a separate personal device, every time.

And if you run a security team, put "our engineers are job hunting" on your threat model. At Binance, that line was worth $6.3 billion.

This follows my earlier piece, Binance Lost $6.3 Billion to Its Own Signing Machine. Details come from Binance's post-mortem of 3 November 2026 and the reporting linked above.

Disclosure: I hold no position in Binance and have no affiliation with the company.

Each editor puts a server part of its own in your home folder on the site the first time it connects. That folder is outside the site, so none of it is served or mixed into your theme.

JetBrains: connect to a remote server from Gateway

#9626. StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents

We’re introducing StateBench, a benchmark for long-context state tracking—how well language models keep track of information about entities in long documents as they evolve.

State tracking underlies tasks from reading code, where variables are assigned and reassigned, to following a story as characters physically move around and objects change hands. For example, if a mystery novel states that “John gave Mary the knife” right before a murder occurs, it’s important to know that the state of each character has changed. However, not all state-tracking problems are created equal: some require only finding the latest update; harder ones require following a chain of changes, where one missed step can throw off the final answer. For example, a harder variant of our mystery state tracking would be if John gave Mary the item in his backpack, with it previously known that Edward put a knife in John’s backpack.

Transformers have well-documented theoretical limits on hard variants of state tracking with long dependency chains, helping motivate recurrent and hybrid architectures such as Gated DeltaNet that carry a running memory forward. Existing state-tracking tests tend to focus on the hardest cases, but as these designs become more common, researchers need to know which kinds of state tracking each architecture can handle. We would like to understand the differences between architectures not just on the hardest kinds of state tracking, but also on the simpler, potentially more common kinds.

To this end, we developed the StateBench benchmark to capture state-tracking problems of different complexity, which we used to evaluate the differences between language models with different architectures. We find that recurrent and hybrid models can generalize much farther than transformers when trained directly on these tasks, while frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna still break down on harder forms of state tracking as inputs grow longer.

StateBench consists of four difficulty levels that permit increasingly complex state update operations. For programmers, these levels of state tracking complexity can be understood as allowing different types of variable assignment operations:

These levels can be intuitively understood in terms of variable assignments, but they also represent theoretically motivated distinctions in state tracking rooted in Krohn–Rhodes theory, a branch of algebra that describes how state-tracking problems – which can be viewed as word problems over finite monoids – can be decomposed into atomic primitives. Each level in our hierarchy corresponds to a class of state-tracking problems that can be built out of a different set of primitives.

To compare the four levels fairly, we start with a general finite sequence of variable assignments and derive three easier versions from it, producing four comparable StateBench problems—one at each difficulty level. All four use the same number of variables and distinct values, with assignments appearing at the same points in the sequence; only the type of assignment changes.

We tested a range of open pretrained models on the r-trivial, aperiodic, and general finite levels of StateBench to see where their state tracking breaks down, and whether different architectures fail where theory predicts. Under standard theoretical assumptions, transformers can handle r-trivial robustly (and soluble and aperiodic to some degree) but are predicted to fail on general problems. In contrast, Gated DeltaNet with a more flexible memory update can, in principle, handle all four levels.

We started with open pretrained models, where the training data and context lengths are fully documented. These included two 7-billion-parameter models, Olmo 3 (a transformer) and Olmo Hybrid (which adds Gated DeltaNet layers), along with smaller models with 275 million and 2.7 billion parameters. All of these models were pretrained on the same data; none had seen contexts longer than 64,000 tokens during training, and we tested most of them on inputs well beyond that length.

When we scored each model, almost all performed well on r-trivial problems, lost accuracy on aperiodic ones as inputs grew, and stayed at chance on general finite problems. Problem format mattered here—the 275-million-parameter hybrid and Gated DeltaNet models scored near the ceiling on RULER-style r-trivial problems but were near chance on the same problems framed as spreadsheet edits. That gap is one reason StateBench tests the same underlying problem in several formats.

We then tested four frontier models – Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna – asking them to read each sequence of variable assignments and generate the final value of every variable.

All four performed well on r-trivial and aperiodic problems. But on soluble and general finite problems, accuracy fell sharply as inputs grew longer, dropping to 13% or lower on the longest general finite problems. One likely factor is sensitivity; at these harder levels, many more steps can affect the final answer, leaving less room for a model to miss an update without getting the result wrong.

Next, we investigated whether models’ difficulty with the harder levels reflects limits of the architectures themselves, or whether pretraining simply doesn’t teach models to solve them. Targeted direct training is a more favorable setting that reveals to what degree state-tracking issues come from the underlying architecture and optimizer rather than the data used to pretrain a model.

We trained several 275-million-parameter models from scratch on StateBench: two transformer variants, two hybrids, and two Gated DeltaNet variants with different memory-update constraints. The models trained on sequences of up to 256 assignments and were tested on sequences as long as 64,000 assignments, or 250 times the maximum training length.

The architectures began to diverge as sequences grew longer. Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models generalized almost perfectly on r-trivial, aperiodic, and soluble problems out to the longest sequences we tested, tens of thousands of assignments. Transformers learned the easier levels but degraded on longer sequences, and they never learned general finite problems. On the hardest level, the Gated DeltaNet variant with a more flexible memory update generalized the farthest, staying near perfect out to roughly 10 times the length of the longest sequences it saw during training.

For Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models, the gap points to training rather than architecture; trained directly, they learned to handle state-tracking levels their pretrained counterparts couldn’t. Transformers were different—even trained directly, they could never learn the hardest level.

Some questions remain open. Our new proof shows that Gated DeltaNet with a more limited memory update (non-negative eigenvalues) can solve all aperiodic tasks and certain periodic tasks, such as tracking whether a repeated input has occurred an even or odd number of times, under the paper’s fixed-precision arithmetic with rounding. Its exact placement in the hierarchy remains open, including whether it can solve all soluble tasks and how numerical precision or combining it with attention layers affects its capabilities. StateBench also assumes a fixed number of variables, while real tasks often introduce new entities over time. In a long conversation, for example, new people and objects can appear as it unfolds, and the model has to begin tracking them too. The current framework doesn’t yet cover that setting.

As new flavors of recurrent and hybrid architectures emerge, understanding which kinds of state tracking each can handle could help guide how future systems are developed and trained. We hope StateBench gives researchers a finer-grained way to find where models break down—and to build training and evaluation data for the capabilities that still fall short. More fundamentally, we hope it serves as a North Star for researchers to develop new architectures with more robust state-tracking abilities compared to current models.

#9624. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

#9622. Building Scalable Webhooks with Cloudflare Workers

Posted on Nov 5 • Originally published at codra.run • AI-assisted

Handling webhooks at scale presents a unique set of engineering challenges. When a third-party service (like GitHub, Stripe, or Twilio) sends an event to your application, it expects a fast, reliable, and secure response. If your server is slow, the provider might time out. If you receive a sudden spike in events, your backend could be overwhelmed.

Cloudflare Workers provide a highly effective solution for this problem. By deploying serverless functions to the edge, you can intercept, validate, and queue webhooks globally with near-zero latency. In this tutorial, we will explore the best practices for building a resilient webhook architecture and introduce Codra, an open-source AI code review engine, as a reference implementation.

When building a webhook receiver, developers must account for several critical factors:

Cloudflare Workers operate at the network edge, running within milliseconds of the user or provider making the request. They offer:

To build a scalable webhook system, follow a decoupled approach. The edge worker should only validate the request and push it to a queue.

Never trust an incoming webhook without verifying its cryptographic signature. Providers like GitHub include a signature in the headers based on a shared secret. You can compute the HMAC signature in your Worker and compare it using a constant-time comparison to prevent timing attacks.

Do not process the webhook payload synchronously. Instead, push the payload to a message queue and return a 200 status code immediately. Cloudflare Queues are perfect for this.

A separate queue consumer handles the heavy lifting. This is where you can implement retries and long-running tasks without worrying about the webhook provider timing out.

If you are looking for a production-ready example of this architecture, check out Codra. Codra is an open-source, self-hosted AI code review engine designed specifically for GitHub pull requests. While Codra supports containerized Docker and Node.js deployments via BullMQ, its serverless deployment profile leverages Cloudflare Workers and Queues to provide an edge-native review loop with zero server maintenance (see the Cloudflare Workers deployment guide).

Codra leverages this decoupled webhook pattern to handle pull request events efficiently. When a developer pushes code, GitHub sends a webhook to the Codra ingestion worker. The worker verifies the payload and queues the review task, ensuring GitHub never experiences a timeout.

Codra focuses on providing a superior developer experience through several key features:

By examining the Codra repository or reviewing its architecture overview, developers can see how to structure large-scale Worker applications, manage secrets, and handle complex asynchronous workflows.

Building webhook infrastructure requires anticipating scale from day one. By utilizing Cloudflare Workers and Queues, developers can build a robust ingestion layer that handles traffic spikes gracefully and processes data securely. Open-source projects like Codra provide excellent blueprints for implementing these patterns in real-world scenarios.

#9621. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

#9619. FlutterFlow Launches AI-Native App Builder for iOS and Android

TechnologyWire (Technology Wire) is a tech newswire and press release distribution platform operated by MediaFuse LTD.

TechnologyWire (Technology Wire) is a tech newswire and press release distribution platform operated by MediaFuse LTD.

TechnologyWire (Technology Wire) is a tech newswire and press release distribution platform operated by MediaFuse LTD.

Mountain View, CA, United States, November 4th, 2026/TechnologyWire/--FlutterFlow today introduced a new AI-native app builder that lets users create, refine, and deploy native iOS and Android applications through conversations.

Builders describe what they want to create, then work with an AI agent to develop the application, connect its backend, and prepare it for deployment to the App Store and Google Play - all within the platform. FlutterFlow's existing visual development platform will continue as FlutterFlow Studio, giving builders direct control over their applications alongside the new AI-first experience.

With the launch, FlutterFlow now supports two distinct approaches to building software: agent-led development and hands-on visual development. Instead of asking builders which product is more advanced, FlutterFlow asks one question: how do you want to build?

“We learned that people wanted a conversational way of building”, said Abel Mengistu, co-founder and CEO of FlutterFlow. “They wanted to prompt for their first idea, and for the changes after. Studio is incredibly powerful, but it didn't give them that experience. We knew that we could build something impactful for this new group of users from the ground up. We also have a fantastic community of millions of builders, built over five years, who want to keep building in Studio. It became clear we needed to build for both.”

The new FlutterFlow takes builders from prompt to production. Its AI agent handles implementation tasks while builders guide the product, refine the experience, and prepare their applications for release.

Both experiences are available at flutterflow.io. New users can select their preferred development workflow during signup, while existing users can continue in Studio and explore the new FlutterFlow through their current subscription, subject to applicable usage limits.

FlutterFlow is an application development platform that helps people build, launch, and manage software. Through AI-first and visual development experiences, FlutterFlow gives builders different ways to create native mobile applications, connect backend services, test their work, and deploy to stores. Learn more at flutterflow.io.

This story was published as a press release by Technologywire under HackerNoon’s Business Blogging Program

#9616. 규제 샌드박스 대 전면 금지: 암호화폐 거버넌스를 둘러싼 글로벌 이분법적 접근

블록체인 기술과 암호화폐의 출현은 전 세계 기존 금융 시스템과 규제 프레임워크에 지대한 도전 과제를 던져줬다.

탈중앙화되고 투명하며 검열 저항적인 금융 인프라를 향한 열망에서 탄생한 이 혁신들은 빠르게 진화하며 새로운 자산군, 결제 시스템, 그리고 비즈니스 모델을 창출했다. 하지만 이들의 국경 없는 특성, 급속한 발전 속도, 그리고 내재된 변동성은 금융 안정성, 소비자 보호, 자금세탁 방지(AML), 테러 자금 조달 방지(CTF), 그리고 시스템적 위험에 대한 심각한 우려를 불러일으켰다.

이러한 다면적인 현상에 대응하여 전 세계 각국은 극명하게 다른 접근 방식을 채택했다. 본질적으로 두 가지 주요 철학으로 나뉘는데, 바로 '규제 샌드박스'를 통한 통제된 실험으로 혁신을 수용하는 방식과 '전면 금지'라는 엄격한 조치를 택하는 방식이다.

이러한 차이는 단순히 규제 선호도의 문제가 아니라, 깊이 뿌리내린 국가 경제 전략, 기술 철학, 그리고 지정학적 고려 사항을 반영한다. 이 글에서는 이 두 가지 대조적인 규제 패러다임을 깊이 탐구하며, 그 배경이 되는 동기, 기술적 메커니즘, 실제 구현 사례, 내재된 한계, 그리고 금융 및 기술의 미래에 대한 광범위한 함의를 분석한다.

다양한 관할권이 선택한 길을 고찰함으로써, 복잡한 디지털 자산 환경을 헤쳐나가는 각 접근 방식의 효율성과 지속 가능성에 대한 전문가적 관점을 제시하고자 한다.

2009년 글로벌 금융 위기 이후 비트코인이 탄생하며 중앙 기관 없이 운영되는 P2P 전자 현금 시스템이라는 혁명적인 개념이 세상에 나왔다.

이 근본적인 혁신은 수천 개의 다른 암호화폐와 블록체인 기반 애플리케이션, 즉 Web3의 발전을 촉발했다. 초기에는 정부와 금융 규제 당국이 이러한 신생 기술을 분류하고 이해하는 데 어려움을 겪었고, 이는 상당한 규제 공백기로 이어졌다.

암호화폐 시장이 규모와 복잡성 면에서 성장하고 소매 및 기관 투자자 모두의 관심을 끌면서 명확한 규제 프레임워크의 필요성은 점점 더 시급해졌다. 몇 가지 주요 동인이 규제 개입을 촉발했다.

첫째, 금융 안정성이다. 변동성이 큰 암호화폐 자산이 전통 금융 시장과 얽히거나 스테이블코인이 적절한 준비금을 갖추지 못할 경우 시스템적 위험이 발생할 수 있다는 우려가 제기됐다.

둘째, 소비자 및 투자자 보호 문제다. 사기, 시장 조작, 불투명한 자금 조달 메커니즘(예: ICO), 그리고 탈중앙화 시스템에서 투자자 구제 수단의 부족은 중요한 안전장치의 필요성을 부각했다.

셋째, 자금세탁 방지(AML) 및 테러 자금 조달 방지(CTF)다. 초기 암호화폐 거래의 인지된 익명성은 불법 금융에 대한 경고등을 켰고, FATF와 같은 국제 기구들이 지침을 발표하도록 만들었다.

넷째, 과세 문제다. 정부는 암호화폐 관련 수익과 거래를 추적하고 과세하는 데 어려움을 겪었으며, 이는 잠재적인 세수 손실로 이어졌다.

마지막으로, 통화 주권 및 자본 통제에 대한 우려다. 일부 국가에서는 탈중앙화된 통화의 등장이 국내 통화 정책을 통제하고 국경을 넘는 자본 흐름을 관리하는 능력에 위협이 될 수 있다고 봤다.

이러한 동인들은 두 가지 지배적인 규제 철학으로 합쳐졌다. 하나는 기술적으로 진보적이거나 글로벌 금융 허브를 목표로 하는 경제권에서 자주 채택됐는데, 기술을 책임감 있게 이해하고 통합하려 했다.

이는 규제 샌드박스의 개발로 이어졌다. 다른 하나는 중앙 통제, 어떤 대가를 치르더라도 금융 안정성 확보, 또는 규제 역량 부족에 강하게 초점을 맞추어 위험을 극복할 수 없다고 보고 전면적인 금지를 택했다.

규제 접근 방식의 차이는 암호화폐가 제시하는 위험과 기회에 대한 근본적으로 다른 평가를 반영한다.

규제 샌드박스는 금융 규제 당국이 설정한 통제된 테스트 환경으로, 기업들이 완화되거나 수정된 규제 프레임워크 아래에서 제한된 기간 동안 실제 시장 환경에서 새로운 제품, 서비스 또는 비즈니스 모델을 시험할 수 있도록 허용한다. 주된 목표는 혁신을 촉진하는 동시에 소비자 보호와 금융 안정성을 보장하는 것이다.

주요 특징을 살펴보자. 참여 기업은 특정 규제 요건의 면제 또는 수정을 통해 기존 규제의 모든 준수 비용을 부담하지 않고도 실험할 수 있어 규제 부담이 줄어든다.

규제 당국은 샌드박스 참여 기업과 긴밀히 협력하며 지침을 제공하고 활동을 모니터링하며 혁신의 성과와 위험에 대한 데이터를 수집한다. 이를 통해 규제 당국은 신흥 기술을 직접 학습한다.

각 샌드박스 진입은 명확한 목표, 제한된 운영 범위(예: 고객 수, 거래량), 그리고 명시된 기간을 갖는 명확한 테스트 매개변수를 가진다. 완화된 규칙에도 불구하고 공개 요구 사항, 보상 제도 또는 노출 제한과 같은 소비자 보호를 위한 명시적인 조치가 마련되어 소비자 보호가 이루어진다.

테스트 단계가 완료되면 기업은 기존 규제에 따라 완전한 인가를 받거나, 새로운 맞춤형 라이선스를 받거나, 제품이 실행 불가능하거나 너무 위험하다고 판단될 경우 운영을 중단하는 종료 전략을 갖는다.

장점은 규제 샌드박스가 새로운 기술에 대한 초기 진입 장벽을 낮춤으로써 혁신을 촉진하는 데 중요한 역할을 한다는 점이다. 이를 통해 규제 당국은 복잡한 디지털 자산과 블록체인 애플리케이션에 대한 더 깊은 이해를 얻고, 시대에 뒤떨어진 규칙을 적용하는 대신 목적에 맞는 규제를 개발하는 데 정보를 제공한다.

이러한 접근 방식은 인재와 자본을 유치하여 관할권을 금융 기술 분야의 리더로 자리매김하게 한다. 또한, 규제 프레임워크를 업계와 함께 반복적으로 학습하고 공동으로 만들어 나갈 수 있도록 돕는다.

단점으로는 샌드박스가 규제 당국에 많은 자원을 요구하며 전문 지식이 필요하다는 점이다. 제한된 범위는 특히 고도로 상호 연결된 탈중앙화 금융(DeFi) 프로토콜의 경우 시스템적 위험을 완전히 포착하지 못할 수도 있다. 또한, 성공적인 샌드박스 프로젝트를 완전한 규제 준수로 확장하는 것이 느리고 복잡할 수 있다는 과제도 있다.

전면 금지는 특정 암호화폐 관련 활동에 대한 포괄적인 금지를 의미한다. 이는 거래, 채굴, ICO 금지부터 암호화폐를 교환 매체로 사용하는 것을 제한하거나 심지어 단순히 소유하는 것까지 금지하는 것을 포함한다.

주요 특징은 금지가 일반적으로 불이행에 대한 엄격한 처벌을 동반하여 금지된 활동에 대한 참여를 억제하는 것을 목표로 한다는 점이다. 이는 명확하고 엄격한 집행을 의미한다.

이러한 접근 방식은 종종 금융 시스템, 자본 흐름 및 통화 정책에 대한 중앙화된 통제를 유지하려는 강한 열망에 의해 주도된다. 주된 동기는 복잡한 규제 개발에 참여하지 않고도 인지된 위험을 완전히 그리고 즉시 제거하려는 위험 제거(인지된)다.

장점을 보면, 규제 관점에서 볼 때 금지는 인지된 위협의 즉각적인 중단을 제공하며, 복잡하고 빠르게 진화하는 기술과 씨름할 필요성을 제거함으로써 규제 환경을 단순화한다. 이론적으로는 자본 유출을 방지하고 통화 주권을 유지하며 시장 변동성 및 불법 금융과 관련된 위험을 완화할 수 있다.

단점 중 가장 중요한 것은 탈중앙화되고 국경 없는 기술에 대한 내재된 비효율성이다. 활동은 종종 지하, 해외 또는 P2P 네트워크로 이동하여 집행을 어렵게 만들고 불법 활동을 덜 투명한 채널로 몰아넣을 수 있다.

금지는 국내 혁신을 억압하여 인재와 자본이 더 관대한 관할권으로 "두뇌 유출"을 초래한다. 또한 디지털 자산 공간과 관련된 일자리 창출, 새로운 산업, 세수와 같은 잠재적인 경제적 이점을 포기하게 된다.

더 나아가, 금지는 종종 기술에 정통한 인구를 소외시키고 기술 발전을 저해하는 권위주의적 조치로 비칠 수 있다.

이러한 상이한 접근 방식의 근본 원인은 종종 한 국가의 경제 구조, 정치 시스템 및 위험 감수 성향과 연결된다. 확고한 금융 서비스 부문과 글로벌 경쟁력에 대한 열망을 가진 국가들은 혁신을 성장의 필수 동력으로 보며 샌드박스 쪽으로 기울어지는 경향이 있다.

반대로 엄격한 자본 통제, 보다 권위주의적인 거버넌스 스타일, 또는 장기적인 혁신보다 즉각적인 안정을 우선시하는 국가들은 전면적인 금지를 부과하는 경향이 더 크다.

영국(금융감독청 - FCA)은 2016년 핀테크 규제 샌드박스를 설립하며 선구적인 역할을 했고, 여기에는 블록체인 및 분산원장기술(DLT) 프로젝트가 명시적으로 포함됐다. FCA는 다수의 기수를 유치하여 기업들이 토큰화된 증권 플랫폼, 블록체인 기반 송금, 스테이블코인 모델과 같은 혁신적인 솔루션을 테스트할 수 있도록 했다.

예를 들어, DLT를 활용한 채무 상품 발행 및 결제 프로젝트가 테스트되어, FCA에 디지털 증권 샌드박스와 광범위한 스테이블코인 규제와 같은 현재 진행 중인 정책 논의에 필수적인 통찰력을 제공했다.

싱가포르(싱가포르 통화청 - MAS)는 지속적으로 자신을 글로벌 핀테크 허브로 포지셔닝해 왔다. 2016년에 출시된 핀테크 규제 샌드박스는 유연성과 반응성으로 높이 평가받는다. MAS는 샌드박스를 활용하여 은행 간 결제 및 정산에 DLT 사용을 탐색한 프로젝트 우빈(Project Ubin)과 같은 프로젝트를 촉진했다.

이후 제정된 지불 서비스법(Payment Services Act, PSA)은 광범위한 암호화폐 서비스 제공업체를 특별히 규제하며, 샌드박스 실험을 통해 얻은 통찰력과 디지털 자산을 금융 생태계에 통합하려는 적극적인 입장을 반영한다.

종종 "크립토 밸리"라고 불리는 스위스(금융시장감독청 - FINMA)는 블록체인 혁신에 매우 우호적인 환경을 조성했다. FINMA는 2019년 DLT 기반 비즈니스 모델을 위해 특별히 설계된 핀테크 라이선스를 도입하여 공공 예금을 받지 않는 기업에 대해 더 가벼운 규제 요건을 제공했다.

이러한 접근 방식은 Sygnum Bank 및 SEBA Bank와 같은 규제된 블록체인 은행의 인가를 촉진했으며, 이들 은행은 디지털 자산에 대한 기관급 커스터디 및 거래 서비스를 제공하여 혁신에서 완전한 규제 승인으로 가는 명확한 경로를 보여준다.

중국은 암호화폐 활동에 대한 포괄적인 금지를 시행한 가장 대표적인 국가다. 2017년 인민은행(PBOC)은 ICO를 금지했고, 이어서 암호화폐 거래소에 대한 단속을 실시했다. 2021년에는 모든 암호화폐 거래 및 채굴 활동을 불법 금융 활동으로 선언하며 금지 조치를 대폭 확대했다.

이러한 결정은 금융 안정성, 자본 유출, (채굴의) 환경 영향, 그리고 사회 및 경제적 통제를 유지하려는 열망, 특히 중앙은행 디지털 통화(CBDC)인 디지털 위안화 추진을 배경으로 했다. 이는 암호화폐 채굴자와 거래소의 대규모 중국 이탈을 초래했다.

이집트와 카타르는 종종 종교적 해석(샤리아 법)과 국가 안보 우려를 인용하며 엄격한 금지를 시행했다. 이집트에서는 중앙은행(CBE)이 2018년 암호화폐 거래 및 발행을 금지했고, 2020년에는 이러한 입장을 더욱 강화했다.

마찬가지로 카타르의 금융 규제 기관인 카타르 금융센터 규제 당국(QFCRA)은 2020년 가상 자산 서비스에 대한 금지를 발표하여 QFC 내에서 암호화폐 자산과 관련된 모든 활동을 금지했다. 이러한 금지는 금융 혁신에 대한 보수적인 접근 방식을 반영하며, 인지된 안정성과 전통적 가치를 우선시한다.

인도(과거 사례, 현재 규제 중)는 완전한 전면 금지를 유지하지는 않았지만, 그 규제 여정은 금지에 대한 강한 유혹을 보여준다. 2018년 인도 중앙은행(RBI)은 규제 대상 기관이 암호화폐를 취급하는 것을 금지하는 회람을 발행하여 사실상 은행 금지를 부과했다.

비록 이 조치가 2020년 대법원에 의해 나중에 뒤집혔지만, 정부는 "사설 암호화폐"를 금지하는 법안을 도입하는 것을 반복적으로 검토했다. 이러한 오락가락하는 입장은 금융 안정성, 자본 통제, 불법 금융에 대한 인도 정부 내의 뿌리 깊은 우려를 강조하며, 결국 디지털 자산에 대한 높은 과세 및 규제 프레임워크로 정착하게 됐다.

두 가지 규제 접근 방식은 그 대조적인 철학에도 불구하고 각자의 한계와 과제를 안고 있다.

가장 중요한 과제 중 하나는 통제된 샌드박스 환경에서 완전한 규제 준수로의 전환이다. 새롭고 맞춤화된 규제를 개발하는 것은 느릴 수 있으며, 성공적인 샌드박스 프로젝트의 향후 경로는 항상 명확하지 않아 실험 후 규제 불확실성을 야기할 수 있다.

전 세계적으로 여러 샌드박스가 존재하며, 각각 약간 다른 매개변수와 엄격성 수준을 가지고 있어 기업들이 가장 강력하게 규제된 환경이 아닌 가장 관대한 환경을 찾는 "샌드박스 쇼핑"으로 이어질 수 있다. 이는 전반적인 글로벌 금융 시스템의 무결성을 훼손할 수 있다.

샌드박스를 운영하는 것은 규제 당국에게 상당한 인적 및 기술적 자원을 요구한다. 복잡한 DLT 아키텍처를 이해하고 새로운 위험을 평가하며 맞춤형 지침을 제공할 수 있는 고도로 숙련된 인력이 필요한데, 많은 규제 기관이 이러한 인력을 갖추지 못할 수 있다.

중앙 집중식 핀테크 혁신에는 효과적이지만, 샌드박스는 진정으로 탈중앙화된 프로토콜(예: DeFi)의 고유한 과제를 적절하게 다루는 데 어려움을 겪을 수 있다. 이러한 프로토콜에는 통제된 환경에서 규제하거나 협력할 수 있는 식별 가능한 중앙 주체가 없기 때문이다.

정밀하게 관리되지 않으면, 통제된 환경조차도 성공적인 샌드박스 프로젝트가 적절한 감독 없이 빠르게 확장되거나 예상치 못한 방식으로 전통 금융 시스템과 상호 운용될 경우 시스템적 위험에 의도치 않게 기여할 수 있다.

블록체인 기술의 탈중앙화되고 국경 없는 특성은 완전한 금지를 효과적으로 집행하는 것을 극도로 어렵게, 심지어 불가능하게 만든다. 암호화폐 활동은 종종 P2P 네트워크, 해외 거래소 또는 VPN으로 보호되는 플랫폼으로 이동하여 모니터링하기가 더 어려워진다.

암호화폐를 금지하는 것은 빠르게 성장하는 기술 분야에서 국내 혁신의 잠재력을 포기하는 것을 의미한다. 이는 기업가와 개발자들이 암호화폐에 더 우호적인 관할권으로 이동하게 만들고, 잠재적인 경제 성장, 일자리 창출, 세수 손실로 이어진다.

암호화폐 활동을 지하로 몰아넣음으로써, 금지는 의도치 않게 투명성을 감소시킨다. 이는 법 집행 기관이 불법 거래를 추적하는 것을 상당히 어렵게 만들어, 금지가 종종 달성하려는 AML/CTF 목표 자체를 효과적으로 훼손한다.

금지는 규제 당국이 기술에 대한 직접적인 지식과 이해를 얻는 것을 방해하여, 궁극적으로 기술의 글로벌 확산에 대처할 준비가 부족하게 만들고 미래 기술 변화에 뒤처질 수 있다.

엄격한 금지는 개인과 기관이 디지털 자산을 보존하거나 글로벌 암호화폐 시장에 참여하려고 함에 따라 자본 유출로 이어질 수 있다. 또한, 이러한 금지를 퇴행적인 조치로 보는 젊고 기술에 정통한 인구층을 소외시킬 수도 있다.

암호화폐 규제에 대한 글로벌한 차이, 즉 규제 샌드박스의 신중한 실험과 전면 금지라는 무딘 도구 사이의 대립은 혁신 촉진과 인지된 위험 완화 사이의 근본적인 긴장을 반영한다. 전면적인 금지는 즉각적이고 피상적인 통제감을 제공하지만, 장기적인 효율성과 지속 가능성은 매우 의문스럽다.

블록체인 기술의 탈중앙화되고 국경 없는, 그리고 검열 저항적인 특성은 본질적으로 완전한 근절을 불가능하게 한다. 역사는 기술 발전을 금지하려는 시도가 종종 이를 지하로 몰아넣어 덜 투명하고 모니터링하기 어려운 생태계를 만들었음을 보여줬다.

이는 결국 제거하려 했던 바로 그 위험을 악화시키는 동시에 막대한 경제적, 혁신적 잠재력을 희생시킨다.

반면, 규제 샌드박스는 내재된 복잡성과 자원 요구에도 불구하고 보다 실용적이고 미래 지향적인 접근 방식을 대표한다. 이들은 디지털 자산의 변혁적 잠재력을 인정하면서도, 규제 당국이 학습하고 적응하며 목적에 맞는 규제를 공동으로 만들 수 있는 구조화된 프레임워크를 제공한다.

이러한 반복적인 학습 과정은 관할권이 강력한 소비자 보호, 금융 안정성, 그리고 AML/CTF 준수와 혁신의 균형을 맞추는 미묘한 정책을 개발할 수 있도록 한다. 영국, 싱가포르, 스위스와 같은 국가들은 적극적인 참여를 통해 디지털 자산 혁명의 선두에 서서 인재와 자본을 유치해 왔다.

궁극적으로 한 국가가 선택하는 길은 그 국가의 광범위한 경제 철학, 적응형 거버넌스 역량, 그리고 기술적 혼란을 수용하거나 저항하려는 의지를 반영한다. 전문가적 관점에서 볼 때, 전면 금지의 즉각적인 매력이 절대적인 통제를 추구하는 이들에게는 매력적일지 모르지만, 장기적으로는 대체로 자멸적인 전략이다.

글로벌 금융의 미래는 필연적으로 블록체인 기술과 얽히게 될 것이다. 따라서 국가들에게 더 지속 가능하고 유익한 접근 방식은 이러한 혁신을 헛되이 금지하려 하기보다는 지능적으로 통합하고 규제하는 것이다. 규제 차익 거래를 방지하고 안전하고 효율적이며 혁신적인 글로벌 디지털 자산 생태계를 조성하기 위해서는 국제 협력과 조화된 규제 표준이 필수적이다.

#9614. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

#9609. A 7-point checklist before you let Codex review Claude Code commits

Claude Code writes, Codex reviews, a gate decides what merges. Here's the short version I check before trusting that loop on a repo. The full walkthrough, with the prompts, is in How to make Codex review Claude Code's commits.

1. Codex runs read-only. codex exec -s read-only --color never --output-last-message -, with the prompt on stdin. The reviewer can read files and run git diff, but it can't write or hand back a patch.

2. One verdict line, saved under the commit hash. Verdict: ACCEPT or Verdict: CHANGES REQUIRED, read only from the --output-last-message file. A crash, an empty answer or two Verdict lines leave no saved verdict, so the commit can't merge.

3. A brief exists before the code. Every line under "Done means" is something a reviewer can confirm from the diff or a test. Write "a customer email with a comma is escaped", never "export works well".

4. Each new test failed on the base commit. The engine that writes the code often writes the tests too. A test that already passes on the old code proves nothing about the change.

5. House rules live where both engines read them. CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, AGENTS.md for Codex. Keep the AGENTS.md part short: Codex stops adding instruction files once their combined size reaches project_doc_max_bytes, 32 KiB by default.

6. The reviewer answers every line. Met with a file:line, not met with what's missing, or not checkable with the evidence it would need. Findings outside the brief need a concrete failure. Style preferences aren't findings.

7. Rounds have a hard cap. Later rounds raise only what blocks the merge. If the last allowed round says CHANGES REQUIRED, the merge stays blocked and a person decides.

The merge is refused unless that exact commit has a test pass and a saved ACCEPT. A test pass alone won't catch a test Claude Code weakened in the same commit, so that falls to the reviewer: what my review gate does with weakened and deleted tests.

If you want the whole setup prebuilt, the Two Engines Kit for Claude Code and Codex is a paid kit I made, built on information gathered since the first Codex and Claude CLIs.

Templates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use.

#9606. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier

In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

Overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. It is important to note that the generated images should be reviewed and used with care, as they may not be entirely original and could be influenced by the training data.

Grammarly is a writing-enhancement platform that uses AI to check for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text. It also provides suggestions for improving the clarity, concision, and readability of the text. It has several features that make it useful for improving writing, including:

Overall, OpenAI Codex is a powerful tool that can help automate the process of writing code and make it more accessible to non-technical people. However, the quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description and it is important to review and test the code before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

Tabnine is a code completion tool that uses AI to predict and suggest code snippets. It is compatible with multiple programming languages and can be integrated with various code editors.

Overall, TabNine is a useful tool for developers that can help improve coding efficiency and reduce the time spent on writing code. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

Jasper is a content writing and content generation tool that uses artificial intelligence to identify the best words and sentences for your writing style and medium in the most efficient, quick, and accessible way.

Surfer SEO is a software tool designed to help website owners and digital marketers improve their search engine optimization (SEO) efforts. The tool provides a variety of features that can be used to analyze a website's on-page SEO, including:

Overall, Surfer SEO can be a useful tool for website owners and digital marketers looking to improve their SEO efforts. However, it is important to remember that it is just a tool and should be used in conjunction with other SEO best practices. Additionally, the tool is not a guarantee of better ranking.

Zapier is a web automation tool that allows users to automate repetitive tasks by connecting different web applications together. It does this by creating "Zaps" that automatically move data between apps, and can also be used to trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

Overall, Zapier is a useful tool that can help users automate repetitive tasks and improve workflow. It can save time and increase productivity by connecting different web applications together. #9604. क्या YouTube के ऑटो-जनरेटेड कैप्शन इतने सही हैं कि उन्हें कोट किया जा सके?

ज़्यादातर YouTube वीडियो में ट्रांसक्रिप्ट होती है, और उनमें से अधिकतर को स्पीच रिकग्निशन ने लिखा होता है। वीडियो के साथ चलने के लिए यह ठीक है। लेकिन किसी पेपर, न्यूज़ स्टोरी या क़ानूनी नोट में कोट देने के लिए सवाल यह है कि ऑटोमैटिक टेक्स्ट असल में कही गई बात से कितना दूर है, और उसके टाइमस्टैम्प सही सेकंड पर इशारा करते हैं या नहीं। जिस वीडियो में दोनों तरह के कैप्शन हों, वह इसका सीधा जवाब देता है।

वीडियो NASA का अपलोड किया हुआ राष्ट्रपति कैनेडी का 1962 का राइस यूनिवर्सिटी वाला भाषण है (WZyRbnpGyzQ, 18 मिनट)। इसमें दो अंग्रेज़ी ट्रैक हैं: एक किसी इंसान का लिखा हुआ और एक YouTube का बनाया हुआ। दोनों को Python पैकेज youtube-transcript-api से लिस्ट और डाउनलोड किया जा सकता है:

हर एंट्री टेक्स्ट की एक लाइन होती है, जिसके साथ स्टार्ट टाइम और सेकंड में अवधि होती है।

शब्द-दर-शब्द तुलना करने पर (लोअरकेस, विराम चिह्न हटाकर, Python के difflib.SequenceMatcher से अलाइन करके) दोनों ट्रैक भाषण के लगभग 95% हिस्से पर एक जैसे हैं:

छह प्रतिशत छोटा लगता है, जब तक यह न देखें कि वे कौन से शब्द हैं। स्पीच रिकग्निशन आम शब्दों पर अच्छा करता है और नामों, संख्याओं और तकनीकी शब्दों पर बुरा, और कोट अक्सर इन्हीं हिस्सों पर टिका होता है:

एक खाली जगह भी है। लगभग 4:47 पर ऑटोमैटिक ट्रैक "both must be" से सीधे "determined and cannot be deterred" पर कूद जाता है। बीच के 28 शब्द, "enterprised and overcome with answerable courage. If this capsule history of our progress teaches us anything, it is that man, in his quest for knowledge and progress, is", उसमें हैं ही नहीं। ऑटोमैटिक ट्रैक में कुछ भी इस खाली जगह को चिह्नित नहीं करता।

इस भाषण की जो लाइन लोग कोट करते हैं, वह 9:18 पर है। इंसानी ट्रैक में यह एक लाइन है, विराम चिह्नों के साथ और एक स्टार्ट टाइम के साथ:

ऑटोमैटिक ट्रैक में यह तीन ओवरलैप होती लाइनों में फैली है, और पहला शब्द पिछली लाइन का है:

ऑटोमैटिक कैप्शन रोलिंग डिस्प्ले के लिए बने होते हैं, एक बार में कुछ शब्द, इसलिए उनकी लाइनें वाक्यों की जगह बोलने के टाइमिंग का पीछा करती हैं। कोट करने के लिए इससे दो बातें निकलती हैं। 9:18 वाली लाइन कॉपी करने पर ऐसा टुकड़ा मिलता है जो वाक्य के बीच से शुरू होता है, और "not" वाली लाइन का स्टार्ट टाइम 9:15 है, यानी कोट से तीन सेकंड पहले। कैप्शन के तौर पर दोनों में कुछ ग़लत नहीं; सायटेशन के तौर पर दोनों ग़लत हैं।

इस मामले में व्याकरण बचा रहा, "they are", उस वर्शन के उलट जो ज़्यादातर लोगों को याद है ("because it is hard")। लेकिन कुछ लाइनों बाद "we are willing" बन गया "we're willing", और ऑटोमैटिक ट्रैक से लिया गया कोट कैनेडी के मुँह में ऐसा संक्षिप्त रूप डाल देगा जो उन्होंने कहा ही नहीं।

osFoundry डेस्कटॉप ऐप का ट्रांसक्रिप्ट टूल, जो उसी कंप्यूटर से कैप्शन लाता है जिस पर वह चल रहा है, यह चुनाव Rust की कुछ लाइनों में करता है। YouTube ऑटोमैटिक ट्रैक को kind: "asr" से चिह्नित करता है, और ऐप पहले इंसान का लिखा अंग्रेज़ी ट्रैक लेता है, फिर कोई भी अंग्रेज़ी ट्रैक, फिर कोई भी इंसानी ट्रैक, और फिर जो भी मौजूद हो:

जब कोई लाइन रेफ़रेंस के रूप में सेव होती है, तो उसका स्टार्ट टाइम लिंक का t पैरामीटर बन जाता है। समय नीचे की ओर राउंड किया जाता है, ताकि वीडियो शब्दों से सेकंड के एक हिस्से पहले शुरू हो, पहले शब्द के बाद नहीं:

9:18 वाली लाइन के लिए यह &t=558s है, उस लाइन के लिए जो 558.9 सेकंड पर शुरू होती है।

बहुत से वीडियो में सिर्फ़ ऑटोमैटिक ट्रैक होता है। तब वह सर्च इंडेक्स है, स्रोत नहीं: उससे मोटे तौर पर पता करें कि बात कहाँ कही गई, वह हिस्सा चलाएँ और कोट ऑडियो सुनकर लिखें। नाम और संख्याएँ किसी दूसरे स्रोत से जाँचें, और ऐसे हिस्सों की उम्मीद रखें जो बिना किसी निशान के ग़ायब हैं। सेकंड तक पहुँचने वाला लिंक फिर भी रखने लायक़ है, क्योंकि उससे पाठक वही जाँच कुछ सेकंड में दोहरा सकता है।

यहाँ इस्तेमाल हुआ डेस्कटॉप ऐप osFoundry डाउनलोड पेज से मुफ़्त है।

#9603. Not Milk: Burgers Are 10x Juicier When You Add This Ingredient

Chefs employ many strategies to moisten burger patties. Some add a dash of mayo for extra fat and flavor, while others swear by heavy cream for juicy patties. Still, there are always more mouth-watering options to explore — like buttermilk, for example. The tangy fermented dairy is often designated for giving pancakes some fluff, but lends advantages when worked into minced meat, too.

The lactic acid in buttermilk functions as an effective meat tenderizer, making a burger that's a touch juicier. The dairy's tartness is perceptible in the taste without overwhelming the palate. You don't need much to revamp a burger recipe; half a cup per a pound of beef is enough to translate buttermilk's unique effects. Simply mix and form the patties like during a traditional burger recipe, folding in supplementary ingredients like onions and breadcrumbs if desired.

Similar results in texture and flavor are also possible with buttermilk powder. The dehydrated version of the dairy is easier to work with, and still contains the signature fat and tanginess, just without the extra water. It effectively creates a crust around meats, making it widely used in Southern dry rubs. Dust a third of a cup onto a pound of meat, and you'll get a juicy burger, while helping seasonings stick. Who knew buttermilk could prove so valuable on burger night?

While the effects are primarily textural, buttermilk impacts the burger's flavor, too. The inclusion adds a lightly acidic and milky taste, setting up for complementary ingredients. You can further lean into the patty's tender flavor by adding breadcrumbs, which yield an extra-tender, meatball-like dish. Consider using a flavored crumb — say Italian-herb — and work onions and pickles into the patty, too. Topped with ingredients like fresh basil and sliced tomatoes, you'll get an extra-juicy burger that's enjoyable even when well-done.

Alternatively, you can steer the tanginess into a more spiced direction. Buttermilk is widely used in Indian cooking to absorb aromatics and the same kind of application works in a burger. Mix in store-bought curry powder or make your own blend using aromatics like cumin, coriander, and ginger. To round out the dish, top with mango chutney or a fragrant chile paste.

Finally, if you'd like to keep your burger rendition on the classic side, consider garnishing with a homemade ranch. The iconic sauce employs buttermilk, too, making a burger rendition flavored with the dairy both inside and out. Optionally paired with a couple of bacon strips, it's a flavorful riff on the dish that's bound to stay moist.
