#9549. Turn Wendy's Chili Into Game Day Nacho Dip With This Ex-Employee's Simple Hack

Wendy's menu includes many items you might expect to find at a fast food joint: burgers (although it uniquely offers square patties), fries, chicken nuggets, and salads. But the chain is also a standout in the drive-thru world, as it's one of the few major brands to offer customers items like baked potatoes and bowls of chili, the latter of which are truly comforting after a long day when you want something hearty and filling. Wendy's chili can also be useful on game day as the base for a single-serve nacho dip, and all you have to do is add nacho cheese and sour cream.

The creator of this hack — a former Wendy's employee — simply adds the two extra ingredients and gives it a thorough stir, so it's an incredibly easy upgrade to pull off. Both the nacho cheese and the sour cream will mix easily into the chili, provided it's still hot, or at least warm, from the restaurant, with the cheese adding richness and the sour cream lending a welcome tang. Together, they also create a creamier consistency that makes it perfect for dipping.

If it has cooled, you might want to give it a quick nuke in the microwave (in a different vessel). If it's not quite nacho-y enough for your tastes, you can absolutely sprinkle in some smoky taco seasoning. Or dress it up with some diced jalapeños for heat, and top it with green onions to cut through all the richness.

If you head to your local Wendy's to pick up the ingredients for this nacho cheese dip hack, you might run into some confusion when ordering the cheese sauce, as some customers have reportedly had trouble purchasing it because employees couldn't figure out how to ring it up. Fortunately, several Redditors shared that the sauce can be found under Sides, then Cheese Menu, where it's listed as Cheese Sauce. With that information, you should be able to secure the goods (for a small fee), and the cashier will likely think you're a Wendy's whisperer.

Now, while you're ordering, it might occur to you to get something to dunk into your makeshift nacho dip. Fries are the obvious choice, and Wendy's spuds are particularly well-suited to the job, since they're slightly thicker-cut than some of their fast food counterparts, so they can stand up to the chunky chili better. In a pinch, the saltine crackers that come on the side make for a tasty way to scoop up the dip, but you'd be remiss if you didn't also consider the acclaimed spicy nuggets, or Wendy's Tendys, the chain's juicy breaded chicken strips.

#9548. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

Find our high-extraction Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour online.

#9547. Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

#9545. Skip Salmon: 15 More Sustainable Fish Alternatives

From Japan to New Jersey, salmon is one of the most in-demand, beloved fish in the world, prized for its rich flavor and succulently flaky flesh. But while it's undeniably delicious, there can be some nuances in how sustainable certain varieties are. Sourcing sustainable alternatives can be tricky, but knowing the right certifications and sources can go a long way toward purchasing the right seafood.

Salmon isn't inherently unsustainable, but an incredible amount of global demand can lead to some less-than-ideal practices. In particular, open-net salmon farms may cause environmental issues, whether that's pollution runoff, unsustainable sources of fish feed, or the spread of diseases and parasites to wild populations. One of the biggest differences between farmed and wild salmon is that wild varieties are often more sustainable, depending on the fishery, and well-managed populations are carefully monitored to ensure long-term viability. Still, New Zealand is famous for its highly rated salmon aquaculture, so it would be wrong to paint all farms with the same brush.

When it comes to sourcing other, more sustainable fish, it's often a solid idea to look for something small and fast-growing rather than something large and predatory. While some certifications may greenwash the sustainability of seafood, guidance from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration can help consumers identify responsibly managed fisheries. Despite salmon's unique qualities, there are many fish out there that are more affordable and sustainable and can still be high-quality substitutes in your regular diet.

If you don't want to change up textures and taste, char can be a more sustainable fish with a mild flavor and fewer calories. As a salmonid, it's remarkably similar to salmon and has the same pink flesh, marbling, and savory skin you've already come to love.

Few fish species are quite as environmentally friendly as responsibly sourced sardines, since they're small prey fish that grow quite rapidly in their first years of life. Fresh, dried, frozen, or tinned, sardines come in enough varieties that there's an option for just about everyone.

Freshwater fish get a bad rap for being milder and leaner than ocean-dwelling species, and responsibly farmed rainbow trout is about as tasty and environmentally friendly as it gets. A thick, skin-on fillet cooked with a pat of butter can be just as moist and succulent, and modern farming practices can be quite eco-conscious.

Tasting like someone managed to cross the buttery sweetness of lobster with a fish, sablefish, also known as black cod, is an ocean delicacy. Even well-managed farming operations can have a relatively low environmental impact, particularly when they use responsible feed sources and strict measures to prevent disease.

Essentially just a giant perch, barramundi is a flaky, versatile protein you can prepare exactly the same way you'd cook salmon. They're a unique case in that they're quite large but can thrive on feeds containing plant-based ingredients, so responsibly managed commercial farming operations can have a relatively low environmental impact.

A catfish may not be much to look at, but they're certainly a lot to taste. As bottom-feeders, they can thrive on an omnivorous diet that includes plant-based ingredients, and while they might be a touch lean, few proteins are quite as good when deep-fried or bathed in butter.

One of the mildest fish you can use in just about anything, halibut is a largely sustainable choice, particularly when it's wild-caught in the Pacific. Atlantic populations have faced steep declines from overfishing, so be sure to source it appropriately.

When you're looking for something to bread, batter, or mix into a salad, few types of seafood are quite as good as whiting. Like other fish, however, its sustainability depends on its source, and some well-managed fisheries in U.S. Atlantic waters are more sustainable than those targeting depleted populations elsewhere.

While mahi-mahi sourced from Central America and southern Asia can be a bit problematic, those caught in responsibly managed fisheries in the Atlantic can be quite sustainable. While the fish can reach a respectable 3 feet in length, they grow rapidly, and their populations can recover quite quickly with responsible management.

Snapper is incredibly delicious, but of all the various species, yellowtail snapper from well-managed fisheries can be a particularly responsible choice. Historically, government authorities and local fishers work together to manage certain populations, helping ensure that these fish are harvested responsibly.

Huge, sweet, and oh-so-fun to reel in, the greater amberjack is a common sight for saltwater fishers looking to make tacos or cut thick steaks for the grill. Strict controls over harvesting wild-caught fish can help protect vulnerable populations, although sustainability varies by fishery, so it's worth checking the source before buying it at a seafood counter.

Sometimes called sunshine bass, this hybrid fish is a cross between a saltwater striped bass and a freshwater white bass. These fish grow quickly and tolerate a wide range of conditions, making it relatively easy to raise them sustainably with minimal environmental impact.

Eating carp can not only be sustainable, but buying invasive varieties sourced from the American South can actually be a boon for the environment! Several species of invasive carp have spread through U.S. waterways, so every bite of their earthy, slightly tangy flesh can help support efforts to protect these delicate ecosystems.

Blackened red drum, also called redfish, was once so popular that it prompted an outright commercial fishing ban in federal waters of the Gulf of Mexico. While responsibly farm-raised red drum can still be a sustainable choice, along with certain wild-caught black drum, it's generally still best to avoid wild-caught red drum, as sustainability varies by fishery.

Fresh, clean, and a premium delicacy, grouper can be a gray area of sustainability. While many species, like goliath, Nassau, and Gulf groupers, face serious conservation concerns and may be illegal to harvest in certain areas, responsibly sourced black grouper can be a great substitute for premium-grade salmon.

#9543. Collard Greens Vinaigrette

For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

#9542. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#9539. Thanksgiving Cornbread

Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

#9538. 4 Wonderful Signs You Have A High IQ

Four things that indicate high intelligence in a person.

Four things that indicate high intelligence in a person.

Being open to experience, cooperative, happy and having strong perceptual skills are all signs that you have a high IQ, psychological research finds.

Of these, being open to experience is a particularly strong sign…

Insatiable curiosity, an active fantasy life, a sensitivity to emotions and an appreciation of art and beauty are all linked to high IQ.

These are all aspects of the major personality trait called ‘openness to experience’.

People who are open to experience are more interested in things that are complex, new and unconventional.

Being open to experience is so powerful that it is linked to intelligence when measured almost 40 years later.

Children who scored higher on IQ tests at just 11-years-old were more open to experience when they were 50-years-old, the psychologists found.

Intelligent people are better at cooperating with others.

While personality traits like being generous and conscientious have an effect on cooperation, higher IQ is the main factor that encourages people to work well together.

People with higher intelligence use more consistent strategies and consider the consequences of their actions.

That is why people with high IQs are so essential: without them society would not work.

The finding goes against the popular idea that being intelligent somehow predisposes people to unhappiness.

The study looked at happiness in the best-known sense of feeling positive emotions and being satisfied with your life.

The results showed that people with the lowest IQ (70 – 99) were the least happy in comparison to those with the highest IQs (120 – 129).

People with high IQs have stronger basic perceptual skills, research finds.

For example, they can tell which way objects are moving more quickly.

They are also better at blocking out background information to make their judgement.

Imagine a ball thrown at high speed — a more intelligent person can pick up its trajectory faster.

A higher IQ makes the brain faster at a fundamental level.

It helps underline that high IQ is about more than just solving puzzles or making the ‘right’ decision.

#9537. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.

Cover photo and food styling by Liz Neily.

#9536. Skip The McDonald's Egg McMuffin: The Fast Food Breakfast Sandwich With Thick, Crispy Bacon

When it comes to fast food breakfast sandwiches, McDonald's remains uppermost in many people's minds. And why not? The iconic Egg McMuffin, with its famously round egg patty, has been the cornerstone of the chain's breakfast menu since the 1970s. And while you can sub the Canadian bacon that comes standard on the McMuffin for regular bacon, Wendy's Breakfast Baconator actually takes the pork product to a whole new level if that's your sandwich protein preference. And more than that, it ranks as one of the best overall fast food breakfast sandwiches, based on the opinions of the customers who eat them.

Wendy's, which has only served breakfast nationwide on a permanent basis since 2020, is doing the morning meat right with its Breakfast Baconator, which features not only six strips of thick, crispy applewood-smoked bacon, but also a sausage patty — which, like the burgers, comes in a square shape — a freshly cracked egg cooked into a patty (Wendy's is one of the rare fast food chains that use real, whole eggs), two slices of American cheese, and a Swiss cheese sauce. Then, everything gets piled onto not a breakfast bread, like a bagel or English muffin, but a potato roll, which is perhaps better suited to hold the hefty fillings. This symphony of flavors and textures led one user on Reddit to call the immensely bacon-forward sandwich "peak fast food breakfast" that "simply just [can't] get any better," a sentiment echoed by plenty of fellow fans.

The Breakfast Baconator is pretty beloved as-is, but there are ways to modify the menu item and make it that much more enjoyable. One Redditor had the idea of actually stuffing more into the sandwich by adding Wendy's seasoned potato wedges and a flavorful sauce, writing that "it'll change your life." We think the Scorchin' Hot sauce would be an especially tasty addition.

Further, if the potato bun is too lunch-y for you, you can swap it out for a breakfast bread — try asking for the Breakfast Baconator on a biscuit. It's a modification that cannot be made on the app or online, so you'll have to verbally request the change when you place your order at the drive-thru or the counter, if your location still offers that option. Of course, if there simply isn't enough of something on the Breakfast Baconator for your tastes, you can add up to four more sausage patties, four more eggs, and extra Swiss cheese sauce.

#9534. 2 Personality Traits Linked To A Stronger Immune System

Certain personality traits influence the body’s immune system response.

Certain personality traits influence the body’s immune system response.

People with more stable emotions have stronger immune systems, research finds.

People who are emotionally stable usually find it easier to control their urges and are mostly unselfconscious.

Emotional stability is linked to being better at dealing with stress and minor frustrations.

Neuroticism lies at the opposite end of the spectrum from emotional stability.

People who are neurotic typically experience more negative thinking and tend to have worse mental health.

The study included 84 people whose response to a vaccine for hepatitis B was tested.

The results showed that people who were more neurotic — meaning easily stressed, nervous and moody — tended to have weaker immune system responses.

Those who were more emotional stable had a stronger immune response.

Dr Anna L. Marsland,, the study’s first author, said:

“The present findings support a link between trait negative affect and an objective health measure — antibody response to vaccination — raising the possibility that individuals high in trait negative affect or neuroticism may have less protective immune responses.”

In a second part of the study, people were given a stressful task to test their immune function.

The results showed that stress tended to lower people’s immune system response — as previous studies have found.

Along with emotional stability, extraversion has also been linked to a stronger immune system, by a genetic analysis.

Extraverts are typically outgoing, talkative and energetic, meaning they tend to interact with more people.

They are, therefore, exposed to more infections.

A stronger immune response may help to protect extraverts against infectious diseases.

Introverts, meanwhile, tend to have a weaker immune response, as do cautious people.

The study included 121 people who were given personality questionnaires, along with genetic tests and general health screening.

The results showed that extraverts had the highest expression of pro-inflammatory genes.

The effect of these genes is to help fight off infections.

Introverts and cautious conscientious people tended to have a lower inflammatory response.

The study was published in the journal Health Psychology (Marsland et al., 2001).

#9533. Heavy cream vs. whipping cream: What's the difference?: Understanding the right cream for your baking.

If you’re baking a recipe that calls for heavy cream, or picking up a carton to turn into whipped cream to finish a dessert, you may be confused when you hit the dairy aisle. There’s “heavy cream” — but also “heavy whipping cream” or, in some cases, just “whipping cream.”

So when it comes to heavy cream versus whipping cream, is there truly a difference?

Aside from being delicious, there are very specific definitions and standards that must be met in order for something to be labeled as heavy cream. It is made by separating the fatty top layer from the base milk layer during processing. The FDA states that heavy cream is cream that contains no less than 36% milk fat.  Comparatively, milk has 0% to around 3% milk fat, as well as a higher water concentration. Because of its fat content, heavy cream retains a rich taste and, when whipped, it excels at creating stiff peaks that hold their shape for a long time.

Whipping cream — sometimes called “heavy whipping cream” — is made using a similar process as heavy cream and is also the milk fat removed before milk is homogenized. However, whipping cream can contain somewhere between 30% and 35% milk fat content, according to FDA regulations. Because of its slightly lower fat content, it whips into a softer, more billowy cream, and it will deflate more quickly than whipped cream made with heavy cream.

Luckily, the difference in taste and performance between the two types of cream are not very discernible. This means you can use them interchangeably in recipes — and it's okay if you accidentally buy the "wrong" one. Both can yield a delicious bowl of homemade whipped cream. (Can’t justify buying a whole carton of either one? We’ve got you covered with an easy homemade heavy cream substitute.)

A note on King Arthur recipes: The King Arthur Test Kitchen prefers heavy cream in most instances, particularly when making whipped cream, because of the higher fat content. That said, you can substitute heavy whipping cream 1:1 in any King Arthur recipe that calls specifically for heavy cream without any issue.

As a general rule of thumb, use heavy cream for making stable whipped cream for topping pies, layered desserts like tiramisu or banana pudding, and any sweet where the structural integrity hinges on the cream really holding its shape. Heavy cream can also be handy for making cream scones and drop biscuits, where the richness of the dairy can shine through. For more heavy cream baking inspiration, check out these 12 recipes that call on heavy cream.

#9531. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

#9530. The Common Vitamin Linked To Weight Loss

The vitamin deficiency linked to increased belly fat.

The vitamin deficiency linked to increased belly fat.

Higher levels of vitamin D are linked to reduced belly fat, research shows.

The conclusions come from a study including thousands of people.

The researchers measured people’s total body fat and abdominal (belly) fat, along with their vitamin D levels.

The results showed that for both men and women vitamin D deficiency was linked to increased belly fat.

However, for women, low vitamin D levels were linked to both increased belly fat and increased total body fat.

For men, though, low vitamin D levels were linked to more belly fat and more liver fat.

More than half of people around the world may be deficient in vitamin D.

Dr Rachida Rafiq, the study’s first author, said:

“Although we did not measure vitamin D deficiency in our study, the strong relationship between increasing amounts of abdominal fat and lower levels of vitamin D suggests that individuals with larger waistlines are at a greater risk of developing deficiency, and should consider having their vitamin D levels checked.”

It is not yet known if low vitamin D levels are causing more fat to be stored or are a result of it.

“Due to the observational nature of this study, we cannot draw a conclusion on the direction or cause of the association between obesity and vitamin D levels.

However, this strong association may point to a possible role for vitamin D in abdominal fat storage and function.”

Vitamin D deficiency has also been linked to cardiovascular diseases, autoimmune diseases and a higher chance of getting colds.

Foods that are rich in vitamin D include oily fish and eggs, but most people get their vitamin D from the action of sunlight on the skin.

That is why levels are typically lower in the body through the winter months in more Northern climes.

The study was published in the journal Clinical Nutrition (Rafiq et al., 2018).

#9529. How to clean cast iron  : It’s simpler than you think.

Despite what you may have heard, cleaning and maintaining a cast iron skillet or Dutch oven isn’t difficult. It’s practically impossible to ruin a well-seasoned skillet, and despite your best efforts, sometimes food will stick. If your cast iron is covered in stuck-on bits of cheese from a batch of Crispy Cheesy Pan Pizza, here's how to clean it.

We can settle the debate once and for all: Yes, you can use soap to clean your cast iron. Dishwashing soap will not damage the seasoning that makes your skillet non-stick. Polymerized oil creates the layer of seasoning through heat, and dish soap isn’t strong enough to break that bond.

No, you cannot clean a cast iron skillet in the dishwasher. This will degrade the seasoning layer and cause it to rust.

You should not soak a cast iron pan either; the water will cause it to rust. If you do end up rusting your pan, you can still rescue it by scrubbing off the rust then re-seasoning the pan.

Using warm, soapy water, scrub the pan with a stiff-bristled brush or sponge to remove any food residue. Avoid harsh, abrasive scrubbers like steel wool or metal pads, which can strip the pan of its seasoning.

Once cleaned, fully dry the pan with a kitchen towel, or place it onto a burner over low heat so the water fully evaporates. Don’t walk away from the pan — it can quickly get smoky once the water has evaporated.

Regardless of which method you prefer, it’s imperative that the pan is fully dry. Water (not soap!) is the enemy of cast iron, which can cause it to rust. Once dry, add a few drops of neutral oil and spread all over the pan with a towel.

A top-tier onion ring brings together several textural qualities into one bite. You want enough heft to encase the slivers of allium, yet a crunchy consistency that's delicate. Each bite should contain both onion and batter, and while seasoning should be present, the onion's internal sweetness should still come through. It's a complex balance to get right, with beer often used as a cornerstone of the batter.

The beverage lends several advantages to onion rings: The hops and malt add flavor, the alcohol evaporates quickly during frying, and — most importantly — the carbonation creates an airy batter that translates to crunchiness. However, if you're not keen on adding a brew to your onion ring recipe, no fear: Sparkling water is a terrific alternative. Just like beer, the carbonation works its textural magic. And when used alongside rice flour (a tempura influence), you'll produce some of the crispiest onion rings, with an even more delicate texture.

It's critical to pour the sparkling water in as cold as possible — temperature control is essential for optimal crispness. As a result, you'll want to incorporate the water right out of the fridge, at the conclusion of batter preparation. Stir until the batter is homogeneous and on the liquidy side, similar to pancake or waffle batter in consistency. And you can also dredge the onions in flour separately first to make sure the breading sticks. Put the two elements together, deep-fry, and you'll get an onion ring rendition that is no less successful than a beer-based one.

Unlike beer and other flavored carbonated beverages, sparkling water's neutral flavor can be used to your advantage. Such a batter comes out lighter and without much added flavor, letting you tweak the seasonings to your liking. A rendition can be kept to a straightforward salt-only seasoning, which really puts the onions front and center. Or you can go with more flavorful spices like onion and garlic powder, paprika, and a dash of cayenne for heat. Apply seasoning both to the batter and after cooking to ensure comprehensive flavoring.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. #9526. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!

#9524. BA’s Best Pumpkin Pie

This pumpkin pie recipe has converted more than a few pumpkin pie skeptics. It’s the kind of Thanksgiving dessert readers return to year after year—and not just on the holiday. The filling is silky and rich, deftly spiced with cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg, and cloves, and tastes unmistakably of pumpkin.

Sweetened condensed milk and a splash of heavy cream give the custard its velvety texture, while maple syrup and vanilla add depth. We use canned pumpkin purée (Libby’s is our pick) for its consistent texture and concentrated flavor. A blind-baked crust, finished with an egg wash, keeps things crisp underneath all that creamy filling.

The trickiest part is knowing when to stop baking. Look for slightly puffed, set edges and a center that still jiggles gently, like Jell-O. The filling will firm up as the pie cools, giving you smooth, custardy slices. Serve with a generous dollop of whipped cream.

Make it the finale in a classic Thanksgiving feast →

Sure. We tested this very filling in several store-bought pie crusts, with good results. Use an unbaked 9" pie shell and blind-bake it according to the package instructions before adding the filling. Packaged crusts may bake faster than homemade dough, so don’t automatically follow the crust-baking times in this recipe.

Yes. This recipe calls for 2 cups unsweetened pumpkin purée. A standard 15-oz. can contains about 1¾ cups, so you’ll need to open a second can. Save the leftovers for another of our favorite pumpkin purée recipes. And be sure you’re buying plain pumpkin purée, not canned pumpkin pie filling, which already contains sugar and spices.

Bake the pie up to a day ahead, let it cool completely, then wrap and refrigerate until you’re ready to serve. For longer-term planning, you can freeze the baked pie for up to 3 months.

2 hours (plus 4 hours 30 minutes for chilling)

Preheat oven to 425°. Roll out 1 disk Perfect Pie Crust on a lightly floured work surface to a 14" round. Transfer to a 9" pie dish. Pick up edges and allow dough to slump down into dish, letting excess dough hang over dish. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Fold overhang under; pinch and crimp. Chill 30 minutes.

Line dough with parchment paper or foil, leaving some overhang. Fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake until crust is dry around the edges and just beginning to brown, 25–35 minutes. Carefully remove parchment and weights and reduce oven temperature to 350°. Lightly beat 1 large egg, room temperature, in a small bowl just to blend, then brush over inside of crust (not the crimped edges) and continue to bake until crust is set and beginning to lightly brown in the center, 10–15 minutes. Transfer to a wire rack and let cool.

Do Ahead: Crust can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and store at room temperature.

Preheat oven to 325°. Lightly beat 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, and remaining 2 large eggs, room temperature, in a clean small bowl just to blend. Whisk ⅓ cup (67 g) sugar, 1 tsp. ground cinnamon, ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ½ tsp. ground ginger, ¼ tsp. ground cloves, and ¼ tsp. ground nutmeg in a large bowl until no clumps remain. Add egg mixture, 2 cups unsweetened pumpkin purée, ⅔ cup sweetened condensed milk, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. maple syrup, and 2 tsp. vanilla extract and whisk until smooth. Pour into cooled crust. Bake pie until edges are set and slightly puffed but center is recessed and wobbles like Jell-O, 60–75 minutes (it will continue to set after baking). Transfer to a wire rack and let cool at least 3 hours before slicing. Serve with whipped cream.

Do Ahead: Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and chill. Serve warm or at room temperature. You can also freeze pumpkin pie up to 3 months in advance.

#9523. The secret to make-ahead pie crust? Pie crumbs.: Get ahead on your pie baking right now.

'Tis the season — to start thinking about holiday baking. And while this time of year is full of joy and celebration, it can also be stressful. We’re all searching for ways to get ahead of the curve, and one of the easiest? Make-ahead pie crust, made using pie crumbs.

I first learned of this technique from a 90-something friend with whom I love to talk baking. Over lunch one day, something she said about pie captured my attention.

"Did you ever hear of pie crumbs?" she asked. I admitted I hadn't — aside from the obvious: the scraps of pie crust left on the plate after the slice is gone. "My mother used to mix flour and salt and lard together to make this crumbly mixture that she'd store in a crock in the cellar. She called them her pie crumbs. When she wanted to make a pie, she'd just scoop out a few handfuls, add water, and roll out her crust."

Sounds like a good make-ahead solution for 100 years ago — but now that we have easy access to freezers, why not just make pie dough and freeze it in ready-to-roll disks? A couple of reasons, actually.

1) Pie crumbs allow you to make any amount of crust, from mini apple pies to a crust for a deep-dish 10" pie. With frozen disks, you're looking at a standard single crust — not always exactly what you want.

2) Pie crumbs save time. Remove however much of the crumbly mixture you need (more on this below) from the freezer, and within 15 minutes the fat is soft enough that you can add water and roll out your crust. Compare that to the hours it takes to thaw and roll a frozen disk of prepared crust — not to mention the elbow grease if your crust isn’t fully thawed.

3) Pie crumbs can be more stable in the freezer than pie crust disks. Why? Because without the added water, no ice crystals form. Ice crystals can damage the flour/water matrix, leading to changes in its structure (which can then potentially lead to changes in your pie crust).

Oh, and one other reason I like pie crumbs: If my friend's mother used them, they were probably a 19th-century kitchen time-saver. And I love the feeling of preserving and carrying forward our American baking traditions — even something as simple as a shortcut for pie crust.

Choose a standard pie crust recipe: Our Classic Double Pie Crust recipe is good choice, but anything that involves cutting fat into flour (lard, shortening, butter, etc.) will work.

Mix flour, salt, and shortening and/or butter: Follow your recipe up until all of the fat is incorporated into the flour. You should be left with a bowl of dry, crumbly dough that barely holds together when squeezed. If using butter, you should be able to see visible chunks scattered throughout the dough.

Weigh the pie crumbs: If you’re making a large batch of pie crumbs, it’s helpful to weigh and label the total gram amount so that you can easily remove the amount of pie crumbs for a single pie crust as needed. Our Classic Double Pie Crust makes 488 grams of pie crumbs; that means 244 grams per single pie crust. Label these amounts on your freezer storage bag.

Bag, label, and freeze the crumbs: Seal pie crumbs in an airtight, freezer-safe bag and place in the freezer, preferably in the back where it won't be subject to warm air wafting over it each time you open the freezer door.

Scoop crumbs out of the bag into a bowl: Whether one crust, two crusts, or one and a half, do the math and measure the crumbs based on your recorded gram amounts.

Let the crumbs thaw for 15 to 20 minutes or so: Wait until the butter chunks feel barely pliable in your fingers.

Add water and mix: Add water based on your original recipe amount, or just enough water to make a chunky mass when mixed. Squeeze and knead the dough briefly; all you're doing here is bringing the chunks together into one solid piece of dough.

Roll the dough, place in a pan, and bake accordingly: From here, your pie crust is the same as any fresh-made crust and can be filled and baked or prebaked for a no-bake filling. (Bonus: Because the crumbs were frozen and remain cold as you work with them, there's no need to chill your rolled-out crust before filling and/or baking.)

Fairly indefinitely, though the longer they're frozen, the more chance they have both to absorb freezer odors, and for the fats to start to go off. I've also found that, after about two weeks in the freezer, I need to add a touch more water than usual to bring the dough together — due to the drying effects inherent in freezing.

With pie season hard upon us, now's the time to try pie crumbs for make-ahead pie crust. Or maybe you have another old-fashioned pie trick up your sleeve? Share your favorite tips in the comments, below.

For detailed ingredient amounts for the crust demonstrated above, see our recipe for Classic Double Pie Crust.

And if you're looking for additional time-saving ways to use your freezer in the run-up to the holidays, check out our recipe for Homemade Brown and Serve Rolls and Apple Pie with Make-Ahead Filling.

#9522. Add Cowboy Candy To Your Next Grilled Cheese For Triple The Flavor

Making the best grilled cheese can be serious business. And though the modern grilled cheese didn't take off until the 1920s — when commercially sliced bread and process cheese made it an affordable household staple — one perfect add-on for your next sandwich carries a classic frontier spirit. It's called cowboy candy — sugared and pickled jalapeño peppers — and each slice adds an incredible amount of flavor to your meal.

If you like the sweet and sour mix of bread and butter pickles, and you can handle a decent hit of spiciness, you'll love cowboy candy. When jalapeños are pickled, the brine can mellow their heat, so you won't just get a blast of intense spiciness. You'll get crunchy, vegetal, and herbaceous notes; some nice tang from the vinegar; plus a hit of sweetness. And it goes with just about any cheese you want to put on your sando. Cheddar or Monterey Jack are classic American options. If you want more nuttiness, you can try Gruyère, or give Havarti a go for some nice buttery flavor that would also be delicious with caramelized onions. And adding some spicy chorizo will make it a full meal.

The history of cowboy candy begins in the Lone Star State. WHH Ranch, which is based in Texas, claims to be the originator of the condiment and the oldest family-owned cannery in the state. These days, you can order a variety of cowboy candy versions from its website.

If you want to make cowboy candy at home, it's not hard to do on your own. You're going to need a mix of sugar, vinegar, and pickling spices. The mixture will cook down into a thick syrup to give the peppers a nice sugary coating that turns a regular spicy grilled cheese into a masterful mix of flavors. For the spices, you can go the standard route with mustard seeds, celery seeds, and turmeric for the tasty bread and butter pickle style. But a little dried or fresh dill will get you closer to a classic dill pickle flavor, and some chipotle pepper powder will add more smokiness. If you want more of a pungent tang, you can add some apple cider vinegar.

When you're making your cowboy candy grilled cheese, think about what cheeses will blend best with the sweet, spicy, savory flavor. Maybe try a nice sourdough or thick Texas toast, and don't be afraid to try some other protein additions. Turn it into a taco-inspired sandwich with some seasoned ground beef, or use up the leftovers from your rotisserie chicken. Just get that cowboy candy for your next grilled cheese, and from there, you can pile on the flavor.

#9521. 10 Best Chain Italian Subs, According To Customer Reviews

The Italian sub is its own category of cuisine. Born of the ingenuity of Italian immigrants, this centuries-old sandwich balances the highest forms of culinary technique with the simplest combination of ingredients. Expertly cured meats, creamy provolone cheese, crisp vegetables, and the right formula of oil and vinegar — all layered on a crusty roll, hoagie, or baguette — meld into a perfectly harmonious bite that's simultaneously salty, tangy, punchy, and fresh. Within this basic framework is room for limitless personalization. Some shops adorn their Italian sandwich with mayonnaise or hot relish. Another might add prosciutto or smoked ham or a stack of vinegary banana peppers. One may even toast the thing.

That's why the Italian sub is such a fun food to explore. No two are identical — even if they use exactly the same ingredients. Obviously, a sandwich with so much history is an easy target for dissection and judgment. Customers have their favorites, especially when it comes to what's offered at popular chain restaurants. And they're not afraid to share their feelings. For this article, I looked through hundreds of reviews, comments, and posts to find the Italian sub sandwiches with the highest customer ratings and feedback. The chains on this list range from dedicated sandwich spots to supermarkets to gas–station chains, but they all put together a great Italian sub.

With higher-quality ingredients, sliced-to-order meats, and lettuce shredded so thin it defies Newtonian mechanics, you could argue Jersey Mike's has successfully redefined the fast-casual sub. But a sandwich shop — especially one with the word "Jersey" in its name — is really only as good as its Italian sub. And in this department, Mike's Original Italian (AKA "The #13") delivers. It's a classic "Jersey-style" Italian sandwich, filled with provolone, ham, prosciuttini, capicola, salami, and pepperoni, creating a symphony of sweet, spicy, and savory meats.

"I went to Jersey Mike's for the first time and had one of the best subs I've had in a long time – #13 Italian sub done Mike's way," starts one Reddit thread. "13, Mike's way, add relish is the best Italian sandwich I have had since buying them from Italian bakeries as a kid." noted another commenter. The overall consensus is that Jersey Mike's takes pride in its product, and that getting the sandwich "Mike's Way," with a topping of tomato, onion, olive oil, red wine vinegar, oregano, and salt, elevates the experience to what you may find at a local Italian deli. It seems the community has spoken: Jersey Mike's is the best.

With over 2,500 locations across the country, Jimmy John's is one of the largest sandwich chains in the U.S., and while not all its sandwiches receive universal praise, one exception stands out: the JJ's Italian Night Club. And just like its major competitor, Jersey Mike's, Jimmy John's doesn't reinvent the wheel with its Italian sandwich. It's a classic combination of meat (salami, capicola, ham), provolone cheese, onion, lettuce, tomato, mayo, oil, vinegar, and seasonings, all served on freshly baked French bread.

Customers love the bread at Jimmy John's — just not its appearance. "Their bread looks plain AF, but it really do hit," said one Redditor. "That bread looks sad, but the Italian night club with hot peppers is the only sandwich that gets my money there," mentioned another. To deal with this boring bread, regulars recommend toasting it to achieve a light-brown crust and accentuate its yeasty aroma. The aforementioned hot peppers are another game changer, adding a tart, vinegary bite and lingering heat that cuts through the otherwise rich and meaty sandwich. One insider suggests that, when ordering the hot peppers, ask for extra.

While Jersey Mike's and Jimmy John's have thousands of locations scattered throughout the country, there are a handful of smaller regional chains serving quality, thoughtfully assembled sub sandwiches. Penn Station is one of them. With over 300 restaurants across the South and Midwest, Penn Station is winning over the hearts (and stomachs) of its customers with a concentrated menu of subs, wraps, hand-crafted sandwiches, and seasonal specials. As with most sub chains, its Classic Grilled Italian is getting the most attention. Along with the typical ingredient lineup, Penn Station uses smoked ham and banana peppers, minor tweaks that add a little electricity to its signature sandwich.

On Reddit, the sandwich receives gushing adoration from regular customers. "Penn Station's Italian sub has a hold on me," starts one thread. A lot of the love has to do with the mayonnaise, which one person described as "otherworldly." But what makes up the bulk of every sub sandwich is its bread, and here, again, Penn Station doesn't falter, with several customers noting its flavor and texture as a main contributor to the chain's overall success.

DiBella's began as a neighborhood grocery store in upstate New York around a hundred years ago. A lot has changed in the centuries since, just not the quality of its sandwiches, which have remained undeniably delicious for decades. Now, I know that we've talked a lot about bread already, but DiBella's might produce the best loaf of the bunch. The dough is aged for a minimum of 16 hours, scored by hand, and baked fresh two times a day to ensure customers never bite into something even remotely stale, which is why one enthusiastic customer called it the GOAT.

Online, people are impressed that the chain can execute mom-and-pop level taste and freshness (and an impeccable meatball sub). "DiBella's is amazing...It's hard to believe it's a chain," noted a fan. But how's the sandwich itself? Well, with a name like DiBella's, you know that its signature sandwich, aptly named "The Godfather" delivers everything you could want in a good Italian sub. All in all, it's a very solid sandwich that needs to be on your radar.

Cheba Hut's branding reads like something from a college dorm room, but its food quality is anything but juvenile or half-baked. Across the board, Cheba Hut does solid sandwiches, but its La Canna has emerged as a fan favorite, with one thread titled "My New Favorite Sub," getting over 100 upvotes on Reddit.

The La Canna distinguishes itself from other Italian subs by using prosciutto in place of the more common capicola, along with Genoa salami and smoked ham. Equally important is the ingredient balance, which pairs crisp vegetables, meat, and cheese with a tangy "shake & house" dressing. "Can't beat a La Canna on garlic herb," said one Redditor. But what makes Cheba Hut so special is its general culture of sandwich lawlessness. There are few rules here; you can get your sandwiches with alfalfa sprouts or cream cheese, on garlic bread, or served alongside a bowl of French onion soup for dipping.

Potbelly doesn't get the respect it deserves. While most of the chains on this list specialize in sandwiches, Potbelly does it all: wraps, salads, soups, subs, chili, milkshakes, mac and cheese, and one of the best club sandwiches around. But with so much variety, it's easy to be fooled into thinking it's a "jack of all trades, master of none" scenario, but this isn't the case at all.

But the Italian sandwich, although slightly more conservative than its other sandwich offering, is still tasty and reliable. Unlike other chains, Potbelly offers four — not three — heavy-hitting meats, including salami, old-world capicola, pepperoni, and mortadella — a detail that only the most observant sandwich snobs appreciate. "Their Italian is the best chain sub shop Italian out there. Nowhere else has mortadella," noted a Redditor. Others appreciate the sandwich, as well, with one person saying it's their "top choice for a commercial chain place." But what really sets this sandwich apart from the others is the giardiniera, a quintessential Chicago topping of hot pickled peppers, carrots, celery, and other veggies. The condiment is so desirable that Potbelly even sells it by the jar.

Unlike some of the other sandwich chains on this list, PrimoHoagies specializes in Italian subs. And that distinction, especially for a Philadelphia-based operation, leaves little room for error. PrimoHoagies is so committed to the Italian sandwich that it offers not one, not two, but five different variations, each with a different formula of sweet, spicy, and sharp meats and cheeses. Online, the sandwiches at PrimoHoagie's are both widely celebrated and the source of debate, specifically for the quantity of meat packed between its bread.

But many customers think this is a good problem and actually appreciate the quantity and value. In many ways, this is the most authentic sandwich of the bunch. It doesn't come with bells and whistles, just a short list of quality ingredients layered on an "award-winning seeded bread." And if you really have an issue with the quantity of cold cuts, just ask the sandwich makers for some extra veggies.

No one thinks twice about grabbing groceries at a supermarket, but for whatever reason, when it comes to prepared foods — especially sandwiches — shoppers are a little more hesitant. But when you really think about it, the supermarket, with its endless inventory of fresh vegetables, breads, meats, and cheeses, is the ideal place to grab a sub. Publix, a chain of grocery stores popular in Florida and the Southern United States, has made a name for itself in the sandwich department. Whereas other supermarkets haphazardly throw their sandwiches together, Publix constructs its subs with care and attention.

Online, customers voice their appreciation. "There are few things better in life than a Pub Sub," mentioned a Redditor. And despite being a regional supermarket chain, Publix has legions of followers across the country who will make a special trip whenever they're nearby. The supermarket's Italian sub, which comes with the classic trio of meats and provolone, isn't revolutionary, but what sets the sandwich apart is the quality of the vegetables and freshly-baked Italian Five Grain sub roll. Add some oil and vinegar for a perfectly balanced bite.

Wawa has a cult following, and for good reason. Its to-go meals, subs, sides, and secret off-menu items are terrific, even compared to fast-casual chains dedicated specifically to the craft of sandwich making. If you're unfamiliar with Wawa, you can order via a handy touchpad, where you can order sandwiches as-is or customize them to your preferences. If you suffer from choice paralysis, its predesigned subs are a terrific option. One that constantly scores high marks is its Italian sub.

In a ranking of all the Wawa subs (or hoagies if you're from Philadelphia), The Takeout declared the Italian the best option, citing its flavorful collection of meats and deft blend of salty, spicy, and fresh ingredients. This is far from a fluke. One Reddit thread dedicated to Wawa's Italian Sub has over 400 upvotes, with users describing their specific orders in the comments. Some people go standard, but many regulars like to add extra meat and cheese, jalapeños, oil and vinegar, or garlic aioli. But it's the entire Wawa experience that has won over the hearts of its customers. You can fill up your gas tank, grab a quick sandwich, and be back on the road in just a few minutes.

Another gas station moonlighting as a fast-casual stop for quality grub, QuickChek isn't so different from Wawa. And the same goes for the quality of its subs. Both chains offer a similar digital ordering platform where customers can choose every aspect of their sandwich, from the toppings to the bread. Sub sandwiches shouldn't leave you hungry, and QuickChek is a bang for your buck. But don't take our word for it. In 2021, QuickChek was named the "Best Value" for Italian subs in New Jersey, according to New Jersey Monthly.

And when you see some of its sandwiches, you'll know why. One of its Signature Subs, the Giant Italian, lives up to its name: a mammoth foot-long sub loaded with ham, salami, pepperoni, fresh mozzarella, tomato, onion, lettuce, garlic aioli, and a dynamite cherry pepper relish. On Facebook, regulars agree that for the price, speed, and accessibility, it's hard to beat a QuickChek sandwich. It's all love for this affordable convenience chain.

I used Reddit, Facebook, roundups, and other social media channels to identify the best Italian subs from popular chains. Some were obvious, but others surprised me. I kept it to chains with more than 50 locations.

If a supermarket or gas station/QSR hybrid reportedly puts together consistently good subs, it made the list. You'll notice a couple of the big names were excluded, and that's due to the fact that it seems that the quality has slipped so low that the general consensus amongst consumers, especially ones knowledgeable/passionate enough to discuss sandwiches on message boards, was unfavorable.
